3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: If the fixed-vector slice is empty there is nothing to prove. Otherwise fix a member $D_0$. Every other member $D$ lies in $(D_0+L)\cap\mathbb R_{\ge0}^r$: its difference from $D_0$ is periodic and has zero marked multiplicities. The integral members of this intersection are bounded. Otherwise enumerate $\mathbb Z^r$ once and for each positive integer $n$ take its first member $D_n$ in the intersection with $\|D_n\|>n$. This specifies the sequence without any choice principle. The nonnegative unit vectors $D_n/\|D_n\|$ have a convergent subsequence in the finite-dimensional unit sphere. Its limit $v$ is nonnegative with norm one; since $(D_n-D_0)/\|D_n\|\in L$ and a kernel of a matrix is closed, $v\in L$, contradicting step 2.1. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We claim $L\cap\mathbb R_{\ge0}^r=\{0\}$. Otherwise take nonzero $v$ in this intersection and let $I=\{j:v_j>0\}$. In the rational linear subspace $L_I=L\cap\{v_j=0:j\notin I\}$, Gaussian elimination gives a basis of rational vectors. Express $v$ in that basis and approximate its finitely many real coefficients by rational numbers closely enough that all coordinates in $I$ remain positive. The resulting rational vector lies in $L_I$, is nonnegative and nonzero. Multiplying by a common positive denominator gives a nonzero nonnegative integral vector in $L$, contrary to admissibility. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For nonnegative chains each $n_{w_i}$ is a nonnegative integer. If their sum is $s<0$ there are none; if $s\ge0$ each coordinate is one of $0,\ldots,s$, leaving finitely many vectors. Apply the fixed-vector result to each vector and take the finite union. If a relative grading identity fixes $\sum_i n_{w_i}$, this argument applies with that integer; it does not establish the identity itself or identify domains with homotopy classes. [step 4.1, algebra] ∎

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Number the regions $R_1,\ldots,R_r$ and identify a region chain with its coefficient vector in $\mathbb R^r$. The condition that its boundary be a real linear combination of full attaching curves is a rational homogeneous linear condition: subdivide the curves at their finitely many intersections, write the cellular boundary of each region on the resulting oriented edges, and quotient the edge space by the span of the full curves, all of whose vectors are integral. Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb Q$ supplies a matrix with rational entries whose kernel is precisely this condition. Append the equations that the coefficients at the regions containing each $w_i$ vanish. Denote the resulting real kernel by $L$. Its integral vectors are exactly the integral periodic domains with zero $w$-multiplicities. Redundant edge subdivisions and equations do not affect this conclusion. [F1, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: A bounded subset of $\mathbb R^r$ has only finitely many integral vectors: a common bound on the coordinates places them in a finite product of finite integer intervals. This proves the fixed-vector assertion. Domains of two disks with the same endpoints have periodic difference: the endpoint corners cancel in their boundary difference, leaving on each attaching circle a cycle, whose integer edge coefficient is constant around that circle and hence an integer multiple of the full circle. Thus the assertion applies to the disk domains in the first paragraph. [step 3.1, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: All intersections lie in a compact subset of the strip interior. Uniform convergence at both ends, and the fact that both limit points avoid the closed divisor, exclude sufficiently long ends. On the remaining compact rectangle, its two boundary edges have compact image disjoint from $E_p$, so continuity excludes a neighborhood of those edges. The remaining preimage of $E_p$ is closed in a compact interior rectangle. An infinite subset would have an accumulation point there, contradicting isolation in step 2.1. Hence there are finitely many intersections. [step 2.1, given]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: At one such intersection, write $h\circ u=(z-a)^r g(z)$ as in [F1], with $g$ nonzero on a small closed disk. The local intersection number is the winding number of $h\circ u$ on its positively oriented boundary in the oriented complex normal line to $E_p$. This is $r$: the factor $(z-a)^r$ winds $r$ times, while $g$ has winding zero because its nonvanishing extension over the disk contracts its boundary loop. Replacing $h$ by another holomorphic defining function multiplies it by a nowhere-zero holomorphic function, which has winding zero by the same argument. Thus the intersection multiplicity is intrinsic and positive. The finite sum is zero exactly when the intersection set is empty. The marked-point domain coefficient defined by this intersection number is that sum. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, algebra] ∎

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The divisor $E_p$ is a smooth complex hypersurface, including at tuples with repeated entries. To check this, choose pairwise disjoint coordinate disks about the distinct entries of a tuple, and use in each cluster the elementary symmetric functions of its local coordinates as coordinates on the corresponding symmetric power. This coordinate description follows directly by associating an unordered tuple to the coefficients of its monic polynomial; conversely its roots, counted with multiplicity, recover the tuple. In the cluster containing $p$, choose its coordinate to put $p$ at zero. The condition that a root be zero is the vanishing of the constant coefficient, which is one of these complex coordinates. Thus near every point of $E_p$ there is a holomorphic coordinate function $h$ with nonvanishing differential such that $E_p=\{h=0\}$. [given, construct, algebra]

10.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Every critical point lies in some $C_i$, so the nonregular values are exactly $\bigcup_i D_i$. Step 9.1 makes this a meagre subset of $N$, proving residuality of its complement. To see density, take any nonempty open subset of $N$, pass to a chart and then a nonempty open coordinate ball with closed ball still in the chart. The closures of the $D_i$ restrict there to closed nowhere dense sets. The deterministic Baire construction of step 1.1 gives a point in this ball outside them all. It is a regular value. The empty-manifold cases are immediate, and values outside $f(M)$ are included because their fibres have no nonsurjective derivative. [F2, step 1.1, step 7.1, step 9.1] ∎

9.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The set $D_i$ has empty interior in $V_i$. If $Q=\{0\}$ in this block, all derivatives are onto and $D_i$ is empty. Otherwise a nonempty product open set $U'\times Q'$ in $D_i$ would, for any fixed $u\in U'$, make every point of $Q'$ a critical value of the finite-dimensional $C^r$ map $v\mapsto h(u,v)$ on its open kernel-coordinate domain. The inequality $r>\max\{\dim K-\dim Q,0\}$ is exactly the hypothesis of [F1]. For $r=\infty$ apply [F1] at any finite differentiability order above that bound. This contradicts [F1]. Thus $D_i$ is closed and nowhere dense relative to $V_i$. It is nowhere dense in $N$ as well: its closure in $N$ lies in $\overline V_i$, and any nonempty open subset of that closure must meet $V_i$, since the boundary of an open set has empty interior. Such an intersection would contradict its relative nowhere density. [F1, step 5.1, step 8.1, cases]

7.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The interiors of all these blocks cover $M$. Choose a countable base $(B_i)$ of $M$. For each nonempty $B_i$ contained in the interior of some block, [F2] selects one witnessing block together with its normal-form neighborhood and target chart. There are countably many such indices, and their chosen interiors still cover $M$: for every point, first use any covering block and then a base member containing the point and contained in its interior. Relabel the chosen blocks $C_i$, neighborhoods $W_i$, and target charts $V_i$. This is one explicit countable-choice use, with the family fixed in advance; no selections indexed by all points of $M$ were made. [F2, step 6.1, construct]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Work in charts about $x\in M$ and $f(x)\in N$, translate both coordinate origins, and write $L=Df(0)$. By step 2.1 split the domain as $K\oplus E_1$, with $K=\ker L$, and the target as $R\oplus Q$, with $R=\operatorname{ran}L$. The spaces $K,Q$ are finite dimensional by Fredholmness, $R$ is closed, and $E_1=K^\perp$. The restriction $L:E_1\to R$ is a bounded bijection and has bounded inverse by step 2.2. Write $f=(\rho,c)$ in the target splitting. The map $$ (v,z)\longmapsto(\rho(v+z),v)\quad (v\in K,\ z\in E_1) $$ has boundedly invertible derivative $(v,z)\mapsto(Lz,v)$ at zero. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 give a local $C^r$ inverse. Shrink its image to a product $U\times A$, with $U\subset R$, $A\subset K$ open. In these coordinates $f$ has the form $(u,v)\mapsto(u,h(u,v))$, where $h:U\times A\to Q$ is $C^r$ and $\dim K-\dim Q=d$. The coordinate changes need only be compatible local coordinate changes; they need not be members of the originally specified atlas. [F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We first establish the needed complete-space facts with the indicated choice strength. Every subspace $S$ of a separable metric space is separable under countable choice: enumerate its ambient rational-radius balls with centers in a fixed countable dense set, and for each ball meeting $S$ select a point of its intersection with $S$ by [F2]. Those selected points are dense in $S$. Complete separable metric spaces satisfy the Baire conclusion by a deterministic construction. Given closed nowhere dense sets $A_n$ and a nonempty open set $O$, enumerate the same kind of balls; recursively take the first ball whose closed ball lies in the preceding open ball minus $A_n$, has positive radius at most $2^{-n}$, and, at the first stage, has closed ball in $O$. Such a ball exists because $A_n$ has empty interior. The centers form a Cauchy sequence; its limit belongs to every closed ball and hence to $O\setminus\bigcup_n A_n$. This uses recursion with a uniquely specified next ball, not dependent choice. It applies equally inside any open subset by keeping the first closed ball inside that subset. [F2, given, construct]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Apply step 1.2 to each real coefficient of $f$, using the modes of step 1.1 componentwise. By step 2.1 the resulting family is an element $u\in H^1_\theta$ and $Du=f$, with $$\|u\|_2^2\le\gamma^{-2}\|f\|_2^2,\qquad \|u_s\|_2^2\le4\|f\|_2^2,\qquad \|u_t\|_2^2\le\|f\|_2^2.$$ For a finite smooth modal forcing the convolution solutions are smooth with exponential tails, so multiplying by cutoffs tending to one also places them in the defining completion; this is consistent with the coefficient characterization in step 2.1. The scalar uniqueness assertion proves injectivity. The estimate $\|Du\|_2\le\|u_s\|_2+\|u_t\|_2$ proves boundedness of $D$, while the displayed bounds prove boundedness of its inverse $Q$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Multiplication by the locally Lipschitz scalar $w=e^{\delta|s|}$ preserves the real boundary conditions and obeys the weak product rule locally. Explicitly $w'=\delta\operatorname{sign}(s)w$ almost everywhere, with no point-mass term at zero because $w$ is continuous. The rule follows first by integrating by parts separately on the two half-strips, whose boundary terms at zero cancel, and then by local $H^1$ approximation, supplied by the finite modal truncations and [F2] in step 2.1. Hence conjugating the weighted problem by $v=wu$ gives $$wD(w^{-1}v)=Dv-Bv,\qquad Bv=\delta\operatorname{sign}(s)v.$$ This also shows that $D$ maps the stated weighted domain boundedly to $L^2_\delta$. [F2, step 2.1, given, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For one component set $\lambda_n=\pi n-\theta$ and $e_n(t)=e^{-i\lambda_nt}$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$. These satisfy the specified real boundary lines, $i e'_n=\lambda_ne_n$, and form an orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1];\mathbb C)$ with pairing $\operatorname{Re}\int v\overline z$. Orthogonality follows by integrating $\cos(\pi(n-l)t)$. For completeness, multiply $v(t)$ by $e^{-i\theta t}$, reflect to $[-1,0]$ by $g(-t)=\overline{g(t)}$, and regard the extension as a length-two periodic $L^2$ function. Its complex Fourier coefficient at mode $e^{-i\pi nt}$ is real and equals $\operatorname{Re}\int_0^1g(t)e^{i\pi nt}\,dt$, precisely the real coefficient of $v$ at $e_n$. Fourier completeness in [F1] proves real completeness, and the Parseval identity follows by the same extension, whose squared norm is twice that of $g$ on $[0,1]$. Moreover $|\lambda_n|\ge\min\{\theta,\pi-\theta\}$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For a real $b\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ and $\lambda\ne0$, define $$a(s)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{s}e^{-\lambda(s-r)}b(r)\,dr,&\lambda>0,\\\displaystyle-\int_s^{\infty}e^{-\lambda(s-r)}b(r)\,dr,&\lambda<0.\end{cases}$$ The absolute value of the kernel is nonnegative with $L^1$ norm $|\lambda|^{-1}$. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|a(s)|^2\le |\lambda|^{-1}\int |K(s-r)|\,|b(r)|^2dr$; integration and [F3] give $\|a\|_2\le|\lambda|^{-1}\|b\|_2$. Initially for smooth compactly supported $b$, direct differentiation proves $a'+\lambda a=b$, hence $\|a'\|_2\le2\|b\|_2$ and $\|\lambda a\|_2\le\|b\|_2$. Approximation by [F2] passes these identities to every $b\in L^2$, with the derivative in the weak sense. There is no other $H^1$ solution: a difference has $(e^{\lambda s}a)'=0$ distributionally and hence equals $Ce^{-\lambda s}$, which is in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ only if $C=0$. To justify the distributional constant assertion, any smooth compact test of integral zero is the derivative of another compactly supported smooth test; a distribution annihilating all such tests is a constant distribution. [F2, F3, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Set $X=H^1_\theta$ and $Y=L^2(S;\mathbb C^m)$ with their real Hilbert structures. The operator $T:X\to Y$ is bounded because $B$ is essentially bounded and both first derivatives are controlled by the $X$ norm. There are bounded inverses $Q_0$ for $D$ and $Q_\pm$ for $D+B_\pm$. For the latter take $\phi_{\pm,j}\in(0,\pi)$ representing $\theta_j-b_{\pm,j}$ modulo $\pi$. The multiplication $U_\pm(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{ib_{\pm,j}t})$ maps $H^1_{\phi_\pm}$ boundedly and invertibly onto $X$, since its derivative is bounded and it maps the endpoint real lines to the desired lines. Direct differentiation gives $(D+B_\pm)U_\pm v=U_\pm Dv$. Thus [F1] provides $Q_\pm=U_\pm D_{\phi_\pm}^{-1}U_\pm^{-1}$. These identities hold on the dense smooth subspaces and hence on their completions. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The range of $A$ is closed. Put $Z=(\ker A)^\perp$. There is $c>0$ with $\|Ax\|\ge c\|x\|$ for $x\in Z$. Otherwise Countable Choice chooses unit vectors $x_n\in Z$ with $\|Ax_n\|<1/n$. Step 1.3 supplies a subsequence on which $K_Hx_n$ converges. The identity $x_n=LAx_n-K_Hx_n$ then makes $x_n$ converge in $H$ to a unit vector in $Z\cap\ker A$, impossible. Given a convergent sequence $Ax_n$ in the range, replace each $x_n$ by its orthogonal projection onto $Z$; the lower bound makes these new preimages Cauchy, and their limit maps to the specified target limit. Thus the range is sequentially closed and hence closed in the metric space $G$. [step 1.3, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Restriction $X\to L^2([-R,R]\times[0,1])$ is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank maps for each positive integer $R$. Indeed partition the rectangle into squares of side $h=1/N$ and replace a function on each square $C$ by its average $u_C$. For smooth $u$, the variance identity and the coordinate-segment fundamental theorem of calculus give $$\int_C|u-u_C|^2=\frac1{2|C|}\int_C\int_C|u(x)-u(y)|^2dxdy\le h^2\int_C(|u_s|^2+|u_t|^2).$$ For the inequality insert the intermediate point $(y_1,x_2)$, bound the square of the sum by twice the sum of squares, and bound each coordinate difference by $h$ times the integral of the squared corresponding derivative along that segment; integrating the other coordinates and dividing by $2h^2$ gives the displayed bound. Sum over the finite grid and pass to the defining smooth completion of $X$. The cell-average map has finite-dimensional range and its error has norm at most $h$. Consequently multiplication $X\to Y$ by any bounded measurable matrix or scalar supported in such a rectangle is a norm limit of finite-rank maps: compose restriction, cell averaging, and multiplication. No extension theorem or general Rellich theorem is used. [F1, construct, algebra]

3.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: In the two formulas of step 2.2, the $i=0$ term involving $B$ and all the terms with $\chi_i'$ are norm limits of finite-rank maps by step 1.2 and bounded composition. For example $\chi_0BQ_0\chi_0:Y\to Y$ uses the compactly supported multiplier $\chi_0B:X\to Y$ after $Q_0\chi_0$, while $\chi_0Q_0\chi_0 B:X\to X$ uses that multiplier before $\chi_0Q_0$. The analogous derivative terms use $\chi_i':X\to Y$. In the remaining exterior terms $\|B-B_\pm\|$ is uniformly as small as desired when $R$ is large. Since $Q_i$ are fixed and the cutoff multiplication norms are uniformly bounded, the sum of those exterior terms has operator norm below $1/2$ on $Y$ in the first identity and on $X$ in the second, for one sufficiently large $R$. Thus $$TS=I+E_Y+K_Y,\qquad ST=I+E_X+K_X,$$ where $\|E_Y\|,\|E_X\|<1/2$ and both $K$'s are norm limits of finite-rank maps. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, given, algebra]

2.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Construct parametrices for $T$ as follows. Choose three smooth scalar cutoffs $\chi_-,\chi_0,\chi_+$ with $\chi_-^2+\chi_0^2+\chi_+^2=1$, the first supported in $s<-R$, the last in $s>R$, and $\chi_0$ compactly supported. They can have first derivatives bounded by a constant independent of $R$: take fixed smooth transitions over intervals of width one at the two ends and use sine and cosine of a transition angle to obtain a squared partition. Their multiplication norms on both $X$ and $Y$ are then uniformly bounded. Write $B_0=0$, and set $$S=\chi_-Q_-\chi_-+\chi_0Q_0\chi_0+\chi_+Q_+\chi_+:Y\to X.$$ The product rule and $(D+B_i)Q_i=I$, $Q_i(D+B_i)=I$ give $$TS=I+\sum_i\bigl(\chi_i(B-B_i)Q_i\chi_i+\chi_i'Q_i\chi_i\bigr),\qquad ST=I+\sum_i\bigl(\chi_iQ_i\chi_i(B-B_i)-\chi_iQ_i\chi_i'\bigr).$$ These hold first for the defining smooth subspace and then by boundedness. Bounded measurable $B$ requires no derivative in these identities. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

1.3.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We record the elementary Hilbert facts used below under precisely Countable Choice. Every closed subspace $Z$ of a Hilbert space has an orthogonal projection: for $x$, countable choice selects $z_n\in Z$ with $\|x-z_n\|^2<a^2+1/n$, where $a=\inf_{z\in Z}\|x-z\|$. The parallelogram identity makes $(z_n)$ Cauchy, because $\|z_n-z_l\|^2\le2/n+2/l$. Its limit $z\in Z$ minimizes the distance; applying minimality to $z+tv$ for all real $t$ gives $x-z\perp Z$. Uniqueness then makes the projection linear and contractive. In particular a closed subspace and its orthogonal complement give an orthogonal direct sum. Also the image of the unit ball under a norm limit of finite-rank operators is totally bounded: approximate the operator within any given positive tolerance and use a finite net for the bounded finite-dimensional image. Every sequence in such an image has a Cauchy subsequence, by taking at each successively finer finite cover the first member containing infinitely many of the remaining indices and then taking the least next index; completeness gives convergence. Countable choice suffices to select finite covers at the countably many scales in advance, and the subsequent recursion is deterministic. [given, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Its cokernel is finite dimensional as well. Let $P$ be the orthogonal projection onto $(\operatorname{ran}A)^\perp$, which exists by step 3.1 and step 1.3. From $AR=I+K_G$ one gets $y=-PK_Gy$ for $y\in(\operatorname{ran}A)^\perp$. Approximate $K_G$ within $1/2$ by finite-rank $F$. Then $\|y\|\le\|PFy\|+\|y\|/2$, so $PF$ is injective on this orthogonal complement. It is therefore finite dimensional. The orthogonal decomposition identifies $G/\operatorname{ran}A$ linearly with that complement. This completes the criterion. [step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The geometric series give bounded inverses of $I+E_X$ and $I+E_Y$. Set $L=(I+E_X)^{-1}S$ and $R_0=S(I+E_Y)^{-1}$. Then $$LT=I+(I+E_X)^{-1}K_X,\qquad TR_0=I+K_Y(I+E_Y)^{-1}.$$ The remainders are still norm limits of finite-rank maps, since composition by a bounded operator preserves that property. Apply the criterion of steps 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 with $A=T$. This proves finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel, closed range, and the promised parametrices, with Countable Choice as the only choice axiom used. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For each positive integer $N$ set $w_N(s)=\exp(\delta\min\{\max\{s,0\},N\})$ and $q_N=w_N'/w_N$, defined almost everywhere. Then $w_N$ is bounded and locally Lipschitz with $0\le q_N\le\delta$, and $z_N=w_Nu\in H^1_\theta$. The product rule, justified on each interval and across the continuous joins as in [F1], turns step 1.1 into $$(D-q_N)z_N=A(z_N)_s+C(z_N)_t+(E-Aq_N)z_N+w_Nf.$$ The norm of the first three terms on the right is at most $(1+\delta)\varepsilon\|z_N\|_{H^1}$. Apply step 1.2 and the assumed smallness to absorb that term, giving $$\|z_N\|_{H^1}\le2M_\delta\|w_Nf\|_2\le2M_\delta e^\delta\|f\|_2.$$ This bound is uniform in $N$; the capped weights make each application legitimate before any exponential integrability is known. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, construct, algebra]

1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For any bounded measurable scalar $q(s)$ with $\|q\|_\infty\le\delta$, the operator $D-q$ has inverse $Q(I-qQ)^{-1}:L^2\to H^1_\theta$ of norm at most $M_\delta$. Indeed $\|qQ\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le\delta/\gamma<1$, so its geometric series converges and $(D-q)Q=I-qQ$. Conversely $h\in\ker(D-q)$ satisfies $h=Qqh$, and the same strict $L^2$ contraction forces $h=0$. Thus this is a two-sided inverse. This argument permits discontinuous $q$ and does not differentiate it. [F1, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: At each fixed $s$, expand $v(s,\cdot)$ in the modes from [F1]. The integration-by-parts and Parseval calculation there gives $\|v(s,\cdot)\|_2\le\gamma^{-1}\|v_t(s,\cdot)\|_2$, because every eigenvalue has absolute value at least $\gamma$. Integrating in $s$ shows $v\in L^2$ on the half-strip. Together with finite Dirichlet energy this makes $u=\chi v$, extended by zero before $s=0$, an element of $H^1_\theta$: it vanishes near the joining edge, and cutoffs tending to one in the $s$ direction approximate it in $H^1$ by the defining smooth boundary-compatible maps. Extend $A,C,E$ by zero to $s<0$. The product rule gives $$Du=Au_s+Cu_t+Eu+f,\qquad f=(I-A)\chi'v.$$ The forcing is supported in $0\le s\le1$ and $\|f\|_2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|\chi'v\|_2$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Finally regard $z(s,\cdot)$ for $s\ge1$ as a curve with values in $L^2([0,1];\mathbb C^m)$. Its squared norm has derivative $2\operatorname{Re}\langle z_s,z\rangle$, first for finite modal sums and then by their $H^1$ convergence from [F1]. There is a sequence $s_n\to\infty$ with $\|z(s_n,\cdot)\|_2\to0$, since $z$ is square-integrable in $s$. Integrating the derivative from $s$ to $s_n$, then using Cauchy–Schwarz and passing to infinity gives $$\|z(s,\cdot)\|_2^2\le2\int_s^\infty\|z_s(r,\cdot)\|_2\|z(r,\cdot)\|_2dr\le\|z\|_{H^1([1,\infty)\times[0,1])}^2.$$ This holds for the continuous $L^2$ representative, which agrees with the given smooth $v$. Multiplying by $e^{-2\delta s}$ proves the claimed exponential $L^2$ slice bound. Dependence of the coefficients on the solution changes none of the preceding estimates, which use only their values and stated bounds along that solution. [F1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: On every fixed bounded interval of positive $s$, for all sufficiently large $N$ one has $z_N=e^{\delta s}u$ and the same equality for its weak first derivatives. The uniform bound in step 2.1 therefore bounds the integrals of the squared function and derivatives on every bounded rectangle by its squared right-hand side. Exhausting the strip by these rectangles proves $z=e^{\delta s}u\in H^1$ with that bound. Its boundary conditions persist, and $s$ cutoffs approximate it in the defining $H^1_\theta$ norm; local smoothness of $u$ and the mode characterization in [F1] give membership in that completion. Step 1.1 now proves the displayed estimate. On $s\ge1$ we have $z=e^{\delta s}v$, $e^{\delta s}v_t=z_t$, and $e^{\delta s}v_s=z_s-\delta z$, proving exponential square-integrability of all three quantities. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The tori and their generators avoid $\Delta$: distinct coordinates of a tuple on a given product torus lie on distinct disjoint attaching curves. The set $u^{-1}(\Delta)$ is a finite set of interior points. Indeed, in local symmetric-function coordinates the repeated-root condition is the vanishing of the polynomial discriminant, a holomorphic defining function, possibly with singular zero set. Near each inverse image of $\Delta$, the equation is the ordinary $J_0$ holomorphic equation because $J_t=J_0$ on $V$. Its discriminant composition is therefore holomorphic. By [F1], its zeros are isolated unless it vanishes on a neighborhood. The set of strip-interior points having a neighborhood mapped into $\Delta$ is open and closed: at a limit point a local discriminant function and [F1] force local vanishing. Connectedness and the boundary condition exclude that possibility. Thus all inverse images are isolated. Uniform end limits exclude sufficiently long strip ends, and compactness of the remaining boundary images excludes a neighborhood of the two strip edges. A closed isolated subset of the resulting compact interior rectangle is finite. [F1, given, construct]

6.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Choose a common regular point $p\in R$ for the finitely many coordinate maps, avoiding the finitely many tuple entries at branch values. At an intersection of $u$ with $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$ the tuple is then off $\Delta$, so precisely one of its entries equals $p$. Each of its $d$ ordered lifts contributes one preimage of $p$ among the $f_l$, with the same orientation sign: $q$ is a local holomorphic diffeomorphism off $\Delta$, and the normal coordinate to $E_p$ is exactly that entry's local complex coordinate. Consequently $$\sum_l d_{l,R}=d\,n_R(u).$$ In particular this signed multiplicity is independent of the generic point within $R$, and agrees with the disk-domain intersection convention. The inverse image of the attaching curves contributes zero to the integral of each $f_l^*\eta$: at points where $df_l$ has rank below two the pulled-back two-form vanishes, while at rank-two points the inverse function theorem identifies this inverse image locally with a finite union of smooth arcs and their intersection points, a measure-zero set. A countable chart cover retains measure zero. Summing the region formulas in step 5.1 therefore gives $$\int_F\widetilde u^*\Omega=\sum_{l,R}d_{l,R}\int_R\eta=d\sum_R n_R(u)\int_R\eta.$$ Combine this with step 4.1 to obtain the asserted energy bound, whose constant depends only on the fixed metrics, taming bounds, and path. Fixing the domain fixes its right-hand side and proves the final assertion. [F2, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

Complete it across each missing interior point by the following explicit local construction. A finite covering of a punctured disk is described by its monodromy permutation: lift a circle and follow its finitely many sheet labels, splitting them into cycles. A cycle of length $r$ is filled by one disk on which $p(\zeta)=\zeta^r$. Near such a point the original map $u$ is $J_0$ holomorphic. In disjoint coordinate disks about its limiting tuple entries, the lifted coordinates are holomorphic roots off the center, by [F1]; they remain in those bounded disks and extend holomorphically by [F1]. The monodromy description follows by lifting radial segments after cutting a punctured disk along one radius; the only identification of the resulting sheet copies is the finite permutation across the cut. No compactness theorem for holomorphic maps is used. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

Set $r_0=1/\sqrt{\max\{b,1\}}$ and $\varepsilon_0=3\pi/(128\max\{a,1\})$. Then $r\le r_0$ implies $br^2\le1$, and $\int e<\varepsilon_0$ implies $a\int e<3\pi/64$. If $e(0,0)=0$, the conclusion follows from $E\ge0$. Otherwise maximize $(r-|z|)^2\widehat e(z)$ on the full closed disk, and let $z_0=(s_0,t_0)$ be a point of positive maximum. 4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: If $\rho<\ell$, one of the nonlinear terms determines the minimum, so $M\rho^2$ equals $1/(16A)$ or $1/(4096c^2)$, or their common minimum when both are present. 1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Reflect the density evenly, $\widehat e(s,t)=e(s,|t|)$, on the full disk. It is continuous and piecewise $C^2$. The reflected integral is $\int_{B_r}\widehat e=2E$. [given, construct, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Apply step 1.2 to $F$ on a radius $0<\rho\le\ell$ about $z_0$; the endpoint radius follows by continuity if needed. The average of $|z-z_0|^2$ is $\rho^2/2$, and $\bigl||t|-|t_0|\bigr|\le\rho$ there. 1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We shall use [F1] also for continuous distributionally subharmonic functions. Here is the needed extension. Such bumps are obtained by normalizing $\exp(-1/(1-|x|^2))$ on the unit disk and scaling. Positivity of the distributional Laplacian gives nonnegative ordinary Laplacian after convolution, since its value is the distribution evaluated on a translated nonnegative bump. Apply [F1] on disks whose closed $\varepsilon$ neighborhood remains in the domain. Uniform continuity on compact subsets makes the convolutions converge uniformly to the original continuous function, so their mean-value inequalities pass to the limit. This proves the stated extension without assuming that a reflected function is $C^2$. [F1, construct]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Apply [F1] with the fixed metric $g$ of step 1.1. Its conclusion and $|du|^2=2e_g$ prove the claimed boundary-center inequality. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

Write vectors uniquely as $a+J_bb$ with $a,b\in TL$, and put $$g_L(a+J_bb,c+J_bd)=g_0(a,c)+g_0(b,d).$$ This is a smooth positive definite form, and $J_b(a+J_bb)=-b+J_ba$ shows that it is $J_b$ orthogonal and that the two summands are perpendicular. In that proof the even reflected density $\widehat e$ has a maximum of $(r-|z|)^2\widehat e(z)$ at $z_0$, with $M=\widehat e(z_0)$ and $\ell=(r-|z_0|)/2$. Its small-energy argument proves $M\ell^2\le4E/\pi$. Consequently $(r-|z|)^2\widehat e(z)\le4M\ell^2\le16E/\pi$ for every $z$ in the full disk. 1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For $D_0=\partial_s+i\partial_t$ and a smooth compactly supported $w$ on the plane one has $\|D_0w\|_2^2=\|w_s\|_2^2+\|w_t\|_2^2$. Indeed the integrated cross term is zero by integration by parts in both coordinates. The same identity holds on the upper half-plane for compactly supported smooth $w$ whose flat-edge values are real: the remaining flat-boundary cross term is the imaginary part of the pairing of the real vectors $w_s$ and $w$, hence zero. Let $w$ satisfy $D_0w=(i-J)w_t+F$ on a patch, with this boundary condition when needed, and let $\chi$ be a real cutoff compactly supported away from the curved edge. Apply the identity to $\chi w$ and commute the cutoff through the equation. The principal coefficient bound gives $$\|\nabla(\chi w)\|_2\le\tfrac12\|\nabla(\chi w)\|_2+C_\chi\|w\|_2+\|\chi F\|_2,$$ so its first term absorbs. This proves the local first-order estimate on any smaller disk or half-disk, with constants depending on the cutoff margin. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We prove uniform local $H^k$ bounds by induction, using slightly nested radii between $\rho$ and one. The $H^1$ bound follows from the given $C^1$ bound and the bounded area. Differentiate the equation once in $s$ and put $w=u_s$. Then $$D_0w=(i-J)w_t-(\partial_sJ+(d_xJ)u_s)u_t.$$ Its forcing is bounded in $L^2$ by the given $C^1$ and coefficient bounds. In a half-disk $w$ has real flat-edge values. Step 1.2 therefore bounds $u_{ss}$ and $u_{st}$ on a smaller patch. The equation rewritten as $u_t=Ju_s$ gives $$u_{tt}=(\partial_tJ+(d_xJ)u_t)u_s+Ju_{st},$$ which bounds the remaining second derivative. Thus $u$ has a uniform local $H^2$ bound. Differentiating twice in $s$ gives the same estimate for $u_{ss}$: its commutator terms contain at most one second derivative of $u$, multiplied by bounded first derivatives, and bounded products of first derivatives. These terms are controlled by $H^2$ and $C^1$. Recovering the other third derivatives from $u_t=Ju_s$ proves the $H^3$ bound. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We first record the elementary two-dimensional inequalities used in the proof. For a smooth compactly supported vector function $f$ on $\mathbb R^2$, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem gives $|f(s,t)|^2\le2\int_{\mathbb R}|f f_s|(r,t)dr$ and the analogous bound in the other coordinate. Multiply these inequalities and integrate to obtain $$\|f\|_4^4\le4\|f\|_2^2\|f_s\|_2\|f_t\|_2\le2\|f\|_2^2\|\nabla f\|_2^2.$$ Applying the fundamental theorem twice to $|f|^2$ also gives $$|f(s,t)|^2\le2\int_{\mathbb R^2}(|f f_{st}|+|f_s f_t|)\le2\|f\|_2\|f_{st}\|_2+2\|f_s\|_2\|f_t\|_2\le C\|f\|_{H^2}^2.$$ These yield local $H^1\to L^4$ and $H^2\to L^\infty$ bounds after multiplication by a scalar cutoff. They hold on half-disks too, away from the curved edge. For $H^1$ reflect evenly across the flat edge. For $H^2$ extend a compactly supported upper-half-plane function to negative $t$ by $F(s,-t)=3f(s,t)-2f(s,2t)$, $t>0$. Its value and first normal derivative match at zero, so the extension is $C^1$, piecewise smooth, has weak second derivatives with no line atom, and has controlled $H^2$ norm. The first calculation remains valid for the continuous, piecewise smooth even extension, which is absolutely continuous on coordinate lines; the second remains valid for the order-two extension because its value and first derivatives match. [given, construct, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For the general induction assume the local $H^k$ bound, $k\ge3$, on a slightly larger patch. Differentiating $k$ times in $s$ gives $$D_0(\partial_s^k u)=(i-J)\partial_t\partial_s^k u+F_k.$$ Repeated chain and product rules express $F_k$ as finitely many products of bounded coefficient derivatives and derivatives of $u$ of orders at most $k$, with sum of their orders at most $k+1$; the sole order-$k+1$ term was separated as the principal term. For $k=3$, the only product not directly bounded by the $C^1$ bound times an $H^3$ norm has two second derivatives, which are $L^4$ by step 1.1 applied to the $H^3$ bound. Their product is $L^2$. For $k\ge4$, derivatives of orders at most $k-2$ are locally bounded by step 1.1. A factor of order $k$ can only be accompanied by total derivative order at most one, and a factor of order $k-1$ by total order at most two; in either case put that high-order factor in $L^2$ and the remaining factors in $L^\infty$. There cannot be two factors of order $k-1$, since $2k-2>k+1$ for $k\ge4$. If all factors have orders at most $k-2$, they are bounded and their product is $L^2$ on the finite patch. This controls every term of $F_k$. Step 1.2 now bounds the derivatives of $\partial_s^k u$, with real boundary values retained. To recover an order-$k+1$ derivative with at least two $t$ derivatives, differentiate $u_t=Ju_s$ $k$ times. Its principal term has one fewer $t$ derivative than the derivative on the left, and all other terms are controlled by the same product argument using derivatives through order $k$. Induction on the number of $t$ derivatives bounds them all. This completes the Sobolev induction. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For each requested derivative order $j$, obtain the $H^{j+2}$ bound on a slightly larger patch from the preceding Sobolev induction. Multiply each $D^ju$ by a cutoff and use the $H^2\to L^\infty$ estimate of step 1.1, including its explicit half-plane extension when needed. This bounds $\sup|D^ju|$ on the desired smaller patch. For any fixed $k$ only finitely many nested radii and coefficient derivatives are used; their constants depend solely on the data stated. All differentiations are of given smooth solutions, so no weak regularity or hidden choice-dependent elliptic theorem has been invoked. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Fix a countable basis of relative strip neighborhoods consisting of rational interior disks and rational-center half-disks along its two physical edges, all of radius at most $r_0$. For each basis member $B$, the energies $E_n(B)$ lie in $[0,E_0]$. Pass to one subsequence on which all these numbers converge. This is an explicit countable diagonal extraction: for a bounded real sequence, repeatedly retain the first closed dyadic interval containing infinitely many remaining terms and take least remaining indices; use that deterministic extraction for the first basis member, then the second, and so on, finally taking the diagonal. Write $e(B)$ for the resulting limit and put $$Z=\{p\in S:e(B)\ge\varepsilon\text{ for every basis member }B\ni p\}.$$ If $p_1,\ldots,p_N$ are distinct points of $Z$, choose pairwise disjoint basis neighborhoods around them. Their limiting energies are each at least $\varepsilon$, whereas their sum is at most $E_0$, since the corresponding finite sums of energies of $u_n$ have that bound. Thus $N\varepsilon\le E_0$. It follows that $Z$ is finite with the asserted cardinality bound. Only finitely many neighborhoods are chosen in this last argument. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For $p\notin Z$, choose a basis neighborhood $B\ni p$ with $e(B)<\varepsilon$. Its actual energies are below $\varepsilon$ for all sufficiently large indices. Choose a smaller disk or physical-boundary half-disk about $p$ whose closure lies in $B$. Step 1.1 bounds the gradients uniformly on a neighborhood of $p$. Finite subcovers give uniform local $C^1$ bounds on every compact subset of $S\setminus Z$. Compactness of $X$ and these derivative bounds give a further subsequence converging locally uniformly to a continuous $u_\infty$. To make the selection precise under Countable Choice, fix finite $2^{-k}$ nets of $X$ for all positive integers $k$, using Countable Choice once for this family, and a countable dense set of source points outside $Z$. At each such point use the fixed nets to extract a convergent subsequence by retaining the first net ball containing infinitely many remaining values, with radii tending to zero, and then least indices; diagonalize over the source points. One may instead use successive finite intersections of the previously retained value sets, so the centers need not form nested balls: their radii tending to zero makes the retained values Cauchy. Local equicontinuity and completeness of compact $X$ extend the dense-point limits uniquely and give uniform convergence on compact subsets, by finite source nets. Thus no arbitrary family of pointwise choices or dependent-choice axiom is needed. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Higher bounds can now be obtained in genuine target charts. At an interior source point choose a target chart about its limiting image and make one constant linear coordinate change taking the limiting complex structure at that point to $i$. Local uniform convergence, uniform first-derivative bounds, and convergence of $J_n$ show that on a sufficiently small source disk all large-index images lie in one relatively compact coordinate set and the transformed coefficient differs from $i$ by at most $1/2$. At a boundary point first take an adapted target chart in which $L_j$ is real and the fixed boundary structure is $i$ along it. Here is its construction: in arbitrary target coordinates write $x\mapsto\ell(x)$ for a local parametrization of $L_j$ and set $$F(x,y)=\ell(x)+\sum_{a=1}^m y_aJ_{b,j}(\ell(x))\partial_{x_a}\ell(x).$$ Its derivative at $y=0$ maps the real and imaginary coordinate vectors to a tangent basis and its $J_{b,j}$ image. Total reality makes it invertible; [F3] gives a smooth local inverse. Consequently $F^{-1}$ sends $L_j$ to the real plane and intertwines $J_{b,j}$ with $i$ along it. At the upper strip edge use the reflected structure from step 1.1. Uniform convergence then gives the same coefficient smallness and bounded image in a fixed chart on a small half-disk. All transformed coefficient derivatives are uniformly bounded on these patches, and the coordinate first derivatives of the maps are bounded by step 3.1. [F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Apply [F2] on every patch of step 4.1. It gives uniform bounds for every derivative on smaller patches. Choose a countable such patch cover, possible by second countability of the strip and Countable Choice for witnessing patches. Extract one subsequence on which coordinate derivatives of every order converge locally uniformly on all these patches: use a countable dense set in each patch, bounded finite-dimensional derivative values, the deterministic bounded-sequence extraction of step 2.1, and diagonalize over patches and multi-indices. Uniform bounds of the next derivative give equicontinuity of the derivatives under consideration, so dense-point convergence is locally uniform. Integrating derivatives along coordinate segments shows that the limiting derivative functions are the derivatives of the already determined continuous limit. The limits agree on chart overlaps because their underlying maps converge to the same $u_\infty$ and the smooth coordinate change obeys the chain rule. This proves all the stated local $C^\infty$ convergence, including the half-disk boundary derivatives. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Pass to the limit in the equation using the $C^1$ convergence of the maps and local $C^\infty$ convergence of the coefficients. Closedness of the compact submanifolds $L_j$ preserves the boundary condition. On every compact subset of $S\setminus Z$, convergence of first derivatives gives convergence of the energy densities and hence an energy integral at most $E_0$. Exhaust the punctured strip by an increasing sequence of compact subsets; monotone convergence gives total limit energy at most $E_0$. None of these arguments controls what happens at the omitted finite set or at either strip end, so precisely the stated compactness conclusion follows. [step 2.1, step 5.1, given, algebra] ∎

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Choose a flat source coordinate about $p$, centered there, with domain a disk or an upper half-disk. At the lower strip edge use the usual coordinate; at the upper edge use $z\mapsto i-z$, so both coordinates are orientation preserving and preserve the form of the equation. Write $f_n=|du_n|_g$ in this coordinate and $M_n=f_n(p_n)\to\infty$. After a tail, choose radii $$r_n=\sqrt{|p_n-p|+M_n^{-1}}$$ smaller than a fixed coordinate radius. Then $r_n\to0$, $|p_n-p|/r_n\to0$, and $r_nM_n\to\infty$. On the compact disk or half-disk of radius $r_n$ maximize $(r_n-|z|)f_n(z)$, and let $q_n$ be a maximum point. Put $\lambda_n=f_n(q_n)$ and $\delta_n=(r_n-|q_n|)/2$. The maximum is at least $(r_n-|p_n|)M_n$, so $\lambda_n\delta_n\to\infty$, and in particular $\lambda_n\to\infty$. On $B_{\delta_n}(q_n)$ intersected with the physical source half-plane, maximality gives $f_n\le2\lambda_n$. All selected points tend to $p$. [given, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Let $v$ be the limit. The equation and boundary condition pass to the limit. Its derivative norm is one at zero in the plane-center case, and at $ih$ in the bounded-height case: convergence is $C^1$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of those moving points. Its derivative norm is at most two by the same convergence, so it is nonconstant. A translation and dilation of a two-dimensional source preserves Dirichlet energy, since the squared derivative scaling cancels the area scaling. Therefore every compact-region energy of the rescaled maps is at most $E_0$, and passage to the smooth limit followed by exhaustion gives $E(v)\le E_0$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: If $p$ is interior, rescale by $z\mapsto q_n+z/\lambda_n$. The domains contain disks about zero of radii $\lambda_n\delta_n\to\infty$; the rescaled derivatives are at most two there and have norm one at zero. If $p$ is a boundary point, write $h_n=\lambda_n\operatorname{Im}q_n\ge0$. Pass either to $h_n\to\infty$ or to a bounded sequence converging to $h\ge0$. In the first case use the same center rescaling; its boundary recedes to height $-h_n$, so the limit domain is the plane. In the second case rescale about the boundary foot $\operatorname{Re}q_n$, obtaining upper half-plane domains on which the derivative bound holds on expanding disks centered at $ih_n$. Every fixed compact upper-half-plane set eventually lies in these disks, and the derivative norm is one at $ih_n$. The boundary values remain on the original fixed submanifold. In all cases the rescaled almost complex structures converge locally smoothly to $J_*(x)=J_\infty(p,x)$: each positive source derivative gains a factor $\lambda_n^{-1}$ and the unscaled source points tend to $p$. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: These rescaled maps have a subsequence converging smoothly on compact subsets of their limiting plane or half-plane. Here the details of [F2] apply without removing points: the global derivative bound two already gives local equicontinuity everywhere. Compact target finite nets and a countable dense subset of the limiting domain give a locally uniform subsequence. In a small disk about each limiting source point choose the fixed target coordinates of [F2], normalizing $J_*$ to $i$ at the center; at boundary points use its explicit totally real chart. Locally uniform convergence and smooth coefficient convergence then give the coefficient bound $\|J-i\|\le1/2$ and uniform coordinate $C^1$ bounds on a smaller fixed patch. The bootstrap in [F2] gives bounds of every order there. Its countable derivative diagonal construction yields local $C^\infty$ convergence on an exhaustion of the entire limiting domain, including boundary derivatives. Thus no concentration point remains in this selected scale. [F2, step 2.1, construct]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Finally choose fixed constants $r_*>0$, $\varepsilon_*>0$, and $C_*>0$ giving the interior center and boundary half-radius supremum estimates of [F1] in the metric $g$, uniformly for every possible autonomous limit $J_*$. This is possible from the uniform coefficient bounds and the two fixed boundary structures; decrease $r_*$ below $1/4$ if necessary. If a derivative-norm-one point of $v$ in the plane, or in the half-plane at height at least $r_*/4$, is considered, apply the interior estimate on a radius-$r_*/8$ disk about it. If its half-plane height is below $r_*/4$, apply the boundary supremum estimate on the radius-$r_*$ half-disk centered at its boundary foot. If total energy is at least $\varepsilon_*$ there is already a positive lower bound. Otherwise the relevant small-energy estimate gives $$1\le\frac{64C_*}{r_*^2}E(v).$$ Consequently $$\hbar=\min\{\varepsilon_*,r_*^2/(64C_*)\}>0$$ is a uniform lower bound for the energy of this nonconstant bubble. This proves exactly the asserted plane or half-plane result, without filling its point at infinity. [F1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Choose $\eta_{m,p}=1/(2K)$. The equation and step 1.1 give $$w_t=R_tAw_t+R_tf$$ as an $L^2$ identity. The real linear operator $R_tA$ has norm at most $1/2$ on both $L^2$ and $L^p$. Therefore the geometric series $$\sum_{k\ge0}(R_tA)^kR_tf$$ converges in each of those spaces. Its partial sums belong to their intersection and have identical distributional meanings: the $L^2$ and $L^p$ multipliers agree on that intersection, because common smooth approximations from [F2] converge in both norms and the multiplier is bounded in each. The two limits thus represent the same distribution. Uniqueness of the $L^2$ solution to $(I-R_tA)v=R_tf$ identifies that limit with the already existing derivative $w_t$. Consequently $\|w_t\|_p\le2K\|f\|_p$. The equation then gives $w_s=(A-i)w_t+f\in L^p$ with a uniform bound, proving $\|\nabla w\|_p\le C_{m,p}\|f\|_p$. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: With Fourier convention $\widehat{\partial_jw}=2\pi i\xi_j\widehat w$, set $$r_s(\xi)=\frac{i\xi_s}{i\xi_s-\xi_t},\qquad r_t(\xi)=\frac{i\xi_t}{i\xi_s-\xi_t}\quad(\xi\ne0).$$ Both symbols are smooth and homogeneous of degree zero, and their first two derivatives are bounded on the unit circle because the denominator there has modulus one. Homogeneity gives the required Mihlin estimates. Let $R_s,R_t$ be their componentwise multiplier operators. By [F1] their $L^p$ norms on the finite-dimensional vector-valued space are bounded by a finite constant $K=K_{m,p}\ge1$, while their $L^2$ norms are at most one since $|r_s|,|r_t|\le1$. For smooth compactly supported $w$, Fourier differentiation gives $w_j=R_jD_0w$. Approximation in $W^{1,2}$ by [F2] proves the same identities for the given weak $w$. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: In the half-plane case let $C$ denote componentwise complex conjugation and extend $w$ by $\widehat w(s,-t)=Cw(s,t)$ for $t>0$. This is a compactly supported $W^{1,2}$ map on the plane. To verify the boundary claim directly, apply the primitive argument of step 3.1 on almost every vertical line; the continuous boundary values agree with the resulting finite-endpoint primitive limits. Since these values are real, the reflected values match, and integrating by parts on the two sides leaves no line atom. Define $\widehat A(s,-t)=-CA(s,t)C$ and $\widehat f(s,-t)=Cf(s,t)$, preserving their original values for $t>0$. Then $D_0\widehat w=\widehat A\widehat w_t+\widehat f$ weakly, since below the line $D_0\widehat w=C(D_0w)$ and $\widehat w_t=-Cw_t$; continuity again removes any distributional boundary term. The coefficient norm is unchanged. Apply the plane result and restrict back. Both the reflected forcing norm and derivative norm gain the same factor $2^{1/p}$, so the derivative estimate has the same constants. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For a local equation multiply the solution by a real smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in a smaller disk or half-disk and extend it by zero. The product obeys $$D_0(\chi w)=A\partial_t(\chi w)+\chi f+(\chi_s+i\chi_t-A\chi_t)w.$$ The cutoff preserves real boundary values, and its forcing has the claimed integrability whenever the displayed localized terms do. The plane or half-plane result proves the local assertion on the region where $\chi=1$. This completes the weak regularity statement, without assuming differentiability of $A$ or regularity of the weak solution beyond the stated hypotheses. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Approximate a given plane $W^{1,p}$ map by smooth compactly supported $f_n$ using [F1]. The last estimate in step 1.1 applied to $f_n-f_k$ bounds its supremum on the entire plane by $C_p\|f_n-f_k\|_{W^{1,p}}$. Thus the sequence converges uniformly to a continuous map $F$. Its $L^p$ limit is $f$, so $F=f$ almost everywhere. Passing to the limit in the two-point estimate proves the claimed seminorm bound. Two continuous representatives equal almost everywhere are equal everywhere, since any point of inequality has a neighborhood of positive measure. No pointwise representative choice at uncountably many points has been made. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]
