3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For the upper half-plane extend $f$ evenly: $Ef(s,-t)=f(s,t)$. This extension belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^2)$, with derivative formulas $(Ef)_s=E(f_s)$ and $(Ef)_t(s,-t)=-f_t(s,t)$, and its function and gradient norms are multiplied by $2^{1/p}$. Here is a weak justification which does not assume a trace theorem. On almost every vertical line, Fubini applied to the distributional normal derivative shows that $f(s,t)$ is represented on finite intervals by a primitive of $f_t(s,t)$ plus a constant: after subtracting that primitive, its distributional derivative vanishes, and every integral-zero test is the derivative of a compactly supported test. Since $f_t$ is integrable to $t=0$ on almost every bounded vertical interval, this primitive has a finite endpoint limit. On a bounded tangential interval the endpoint values are integrable: the primitive formula bounds their absolute values by $\int_0^1(|f|+|f_t|)dt$ after reducing to a unit-height rectangle. Its even extension matches that endpoint and the two integrations by parts have cancelling boundary terms. This proves the normal derivative formula. For the tangential formula, pair tests on the two half-planes and use the original weak tangential derivative; cut the paired test off for $t<\varepsilon$. No derivative of this cutoff occurs in the tangential integration, so convergence in $L^p$ gives the formula as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The plane result restricted to the closed half-plane now supplies the representative and estimate. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph:
Rescale the local disk or half-disk to radius two. Choose a fixed smooth real cutoff $\chi$ equal to one on the radius-one closed disk and supported in the radius-two disk. Multiplication by $\chi$ and extension by zero gives a plane $W^{1,p}$ map in the disk case, or a half-plane $W^{1,p}$ map in the half-disk case. This follows directly from the weak product rule, because the cutoff vanishes in a neighborhood of the circular edge; at the physical straight edge no zero extension is used. Its norm is at most $C(\|f\|_p+\|
abla f\|_p)$ on the original radius-two domain. Steps 1.1 through 3.1 give the unit-scale supremum and seminorm bound. Scaling back uses $\|f(r\cdot)\|_p=r^{-2/p}\|f\|_p$ and $\|
abla(f(r\cdot))\|_p=r^{1-2/p}\|
abla f\|_p$, proving precisely the displayed local estimate. Representatives on overlapping smaller domains agree by their almost-everywhere equality and continuity. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Finally let $f\in W^{2,p}$ locally. Apply the local result to $f$ and each weak first derivative to obtain continuous representatives $F,G_s,G_t$ with the asserted Holder bounds on smaller domains. The distributional equalities $\partial_jF=G_j$ imply classical differentiability in the interior: convolution on an interior disk gives smooth functions whose values and first derivatives converge locally uniformly to $F,G_j$, and the fundamental theorem along segments passes to their limits. In a half-disk the resulting first derivatives extend continuously to the straight boundary; the fundamental theorem on interior segments passes to boundary segments by translation into the half-plane and continuity. Thus the representative is $C^1$ up to that boundary, with first derivatives $G_j$ there and their $C^{0,\alpha}$ bounds. This proves the last assertion under exactly Countable Choice. [step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Work near one source point $z_0$. A constant real target change makes $J(z_0,u(z_0))=i$. At an interior point choose a real basis $e_1,Je_1,\ldots,e_m,Je_m$ successively in this finite-dimensional complex vector space. At a boundary point take a real basis $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ of the boundary plane; total reality makes $e_1,\ldots,e_m,Je_1,\ldots,Je_m$ a basis, and the change sending these vectors to the standard real and imaginary bases preserves the real boundary plane. Continuity of $u$ and smoothness of $J$ then give a disk or half-disk on which $$A(s,t)=i-J(s,t,u(s,t)),\qquad \|A\|_\infty<\min\{\eta_{m,8},\eta_{m,4}\}.$$ The equation becomes $D_0u=A u_t$. After further shrinking its image is in a compact subset of a convex target coordinate ball. All smooth coefficient derivatives are bounded there. Real cutoffs preserve the boundary condition. [given, construct, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Apply [F1] with $p=8$ to a real-cutoff localization of $u$. Its forcing is $(\chi_s+i\chi_t-A\chi_t)u$, which is bounded and compactly supported because $u$ is continuous. The localized map is already $W^{1,2}$, and is continuous and real on the physical boundary. Thus $u\in W^{1,8}$ on a smaller patch. Step 2.1 implies $A\in W^{1,8}$ there. For each sufficiently small nonzero tangential shift $h$, put $v_h=\delta_su$ and $A_h(s,t)=A(s+h,t)$. Subtracting the equations gives $$D_0v_h=A_h(v_h)_t+(\delta_s A)u_t.$$ The last term has a uniform $L^4$ bound by Holder and [F2], since its factors have uniformly bounded $L^8$ norms. The local $L^4$ norm of $v_h$ is uniformly bounded by the tangential quotient estimate. Each $v_h$ separately is continuous, real on the boundary, and $W^{1,2}$: it is a difference of translates of a $W^{1,8}$ map divided by a fixed nonzero number. Therefore [F1] with $p=4$ and a fixed cutoff gives uniform $L^4$ bounds for $(v_h)_s,(v_h)_t$ on a still smaller patch; all forcing terms, including cutoff terms, lie in $L^4\cap L^2$ by finite support. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Apply the converse in [F2] to $u_s$ and $u_t$, whose tangential quotients are the uniformly bounded derivatives of $v_h$. It follows that $u_{ss},u_{st}\in L^4$. The original equation equivalently says $u_t=J(s,t,u)u_s$, since $J^2=-I$. Differentiate this weakly in $t$ using step 2.1: $$u_{tt}=(J_t+J_xu_t)u_s+J u_{st}.$$ Here $J_t$ denotes its explicit source derivative. Both first derivatives of $u$ are in $L^8$, so the product term lies in $L^4$; the other terms do too. Thus $u\in W^{2,4}$ locally. By [F3], $u$ is now $C^{1,1/2}$ on smaller patches up to the physical boundary, with bounded first derivatives. In particular its classical tangential boundary derivative is real. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We record the weak calculus used below. For a continuous $W^{1,q}$ map, the chain rule $\partial_j H(z,u)=H_{z_j}(z,u)+H_x(z,u)\partial_j u$ holds for a smooth $H$ with bounded derivatives on its localized image. Indeed, on interior compact subsets mollify $u$: uniform convergence follows from continuity, convergence of derivatives holds in $L^q$, and the classical chain rule passes to distributions by boundedness and uniform convergence of the coefficient derivatives. This gives the formula everywhere in the open half-domain too; its bounds extend to the boundary because the formula has an integrable right side on the full half-domain. The product rule follows by the same argument whenever one factor and the relevant lower derivatives are bounded, or by Holder when the two differentiated factors have conjugate product integrability. Higher chain and product formulas follow inductively once the corresponding lower derivatives have these bounds. Difference quotients obey $\delta_s(fg)=f(s+h,t)\delta_s g+(\delta_s f)g$, and [F2] bounds the quotients by the weak derivatives on a slightly larger patch. These arguments use countably many mollifications and no selection of weakly convergent subsequences. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

7.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Recover the other derivatives from $u_t=Ju_s$. For a derivative of total order $k+1$ with $b\ge2$ normal derivatives, apply $\partial_s^{k+1-b}\partial_t^{b-1}$ to this equation. The term in which no derivative hits $J$ is $J\partial_s^{k+2-b}\partial_t^{b-1}u$, already known by induction on $b$. In every other product, derivatives of $u$ have order at most $k$, and differentiated coefficient factors have order at most $k$. If a factor has order $k$, it is the only such factor and all others are bounded; otherwise all factors are bounded. Thus all these terms lie in $L^4$ on a bounded smaller patch. For precision, first differentiate the equation only $k-1$ times, by $\partial_s^{k+1-b}\partial_t^{b-2}$, and then take one more weak $t$ derivative. The highest differentiated $u_s$ factor has a known weak $t$ derivative by the induction on $b$; its coefficient $J$ is $C^1$, so the ordinary first-order weak product rule applies. All other factors have the bounded or $L^4$ derivatives just described. This justifies the displayed expansion without multiplying an undefined high-order distribution by a nonsmooth coefficient, and proves the desired derivative exists in $L^4$. Induction on $b$ proves $u\in W^{k+1,4}$. [step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

6.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Take tangential quotients of the last equation: $$D_0(\delta_s v)=A_h\partial_t(\delta_s v)+(\delta_s A)v_t+\delta_sG.$$ The quotient forcing is uniformly $L^4$ on smaller patches: $\delta_sA$ is uniformly bounded by the bounded classical first derivative of $A$, $v_t\in L^4$, and $\delta_sG$ is controlled by $G_s\in L^4$ and [F2]. Also $\delta_s v$ is uniformly $L^4$ by $v_s\in L^4$. For each fixed $h$ it is continuous, real on the boundary, and $W^{1,2}$ on bounded patches, so [F1] and cutoffs give uniform $L^4$ bounds for its first derivatives. The converse in [F2] gives $\partial_s^{k+1}u,\partial_t\partial_s^k u\in L^4$. This supplies the derivatives of total order $k+1$ with zero or one normal derivative. [F1, F2, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

8.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Starting with step 4.1, steps 5.1 through 7.1 prove local $W^{k,4}$ for every finite $k$, using nested patches inside the original coordinate neighborhood. To obtain a fixed neighborhood for any specified order, choose its finitely many nested patches between that neighborhood and a larger one; no uniform positive loss after infinitely many inductions is needed. Applying [F3] to each derivative then gives classical derivatives of every order, with their continuous extensions to the straight boundary and the usual tangential boundary derivatives. The given continuous representative agrees with each Sobolev representative. The equation therefore holds classically and $u$ is smooth as asserted. This conclusion requires the initial continuity premise and does not establish it at any puncture. [F3, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, construct] ∎

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: By the inverse homeomorphism of $F$, steps 3.2 and 4.1 give a unique continuous extension of $u$ to the puncture, with value on $L$ in the boundary case. Localize now in a smooth target chart about that limiting value; in the boundary case use any smooth submanifold chart flattening $L$ to $\mathbb R^m$. The transformed map is continuous and has square-integrable first derivatives off zero. It belongs to $W^{1,2}$ across zero. For the interior assertion, multiply a compact test by a radial cutoff vanishing on radius $\varepsilon$ and equal to one outside radius $2\varepsilon$. In integration by parts the cutoff-error term is at most $C\|u\|_\infty\|\varphi\|_\infty\varepsilon$, since the cutoff gradient has $L^1$ norm $O(\varepsilon)$. All other terms converge by integrability. This proves the weak derivative identity on the whole disk with the original $L^2$ derivative. On a half-disk the identical cutoff argument works, or one can note that zero lies on its physical boundary and the weak identities in its open interior are already available with finite $L^2$ norm up to that edge. The equation holds almost everywhere and hence weakly after filling the measure-zero point. [step 1.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

2.3.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Set $V=F\circ v$, and define $$e(\sigma)=\int_I|V_\tau(\sigma,\tau)|^2d\tau,\qquad b(\sigma)=\frac1{|I|}\int_I V(\sigma,\tau)d\tau,$$ where $I$ is one angular period or $[0,\pi]$. Then $\int_S^\infty e(\sigma)d\sigma<\infty$, $e(\sigma)\to0$, and $$\sup_\tau|V(\sigma,\tau)-b(\sigma)|\le C\sqrt{e(\sigma)}\longrightarrow0.$$ The last estimate follows from the fundamental theorem on the angular interval, Holder, and averaging. In particular every angular slice has vanishing diameter. The map $b$ is smooth for finite $\sigma$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

7.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Finally, for an autonomous plane solution use the holomorphic coordinate $z=1/w$ at infinity; conformal invariance preserves finite energy and produces a punctured-disk solution of the same autonomous equation. The proved interior assertion fills it and gives a sphere map. For an upper-half-plane solution use $z=-1/w$, which preserves the upper half-plane and its real boundary; the boundary assertion fills infinity. The upper half-plane together with that point is smoothly conformally a closed disk, as is seen explicitly by a Mobius map from the half-plane to the disk. All other finite boundary points were already smooth. These are statements about one finite-energy map; they do not infer compactification, no-neck convergence, or gluing for a sequence. [step 1.2, step 6.1, construct, algebra] ∎

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: In the boundary case $a=V(\sigma,0)$ and $a'=V(\sigma,\pi)$ lie in $F(L)$. For large $\sigma$, step 2.3 puts $b(\sigma)$ in the neighborhood of the retraction $R$. The same calculation now gives $$b'=-\frac1\pi K(0,a)(a'-a)+q,\qquad |q|\le C e(\sigma)+C e^{-\sigma}\sqrt{e(\sigma)}.$$ Let $c(\sigma)=R(b(\sigma))\in F(L)$. By step 3.1 and $|a'-a|+|b-a|\le C\sqrt{e(\sigma)}$, $$|dR_bK(0,a)(a'-a)|\le C\bigl(|a'-a|^2+|b-a|\,|a'-a|\bigr)\le C e(\sigma).$$ Boundedness of $dR$ therefore gives the same integrable bound for $|c'|$. Thus $c(\sigma)$ converges to a point of compact $F(L)$. Moreover $|b-c|\le C|b-a|\to0$, since $R(a)=a$, and step 2.3 proves that every $V(\sigma,\tau)$ converges uniformly to that same point. The endpoint contribution has been estimated quadratically, rather than discarded. [step 2.2, step 3.1, step 2.3, algebra]

1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Use cylindrical coordinates $z=-e^{-\sigma-i\tau}$ about the puncture and put $v(\sigma,\tau)=u(-e^{-\sigma-i\tau})$. The angular variable has period $2\pi$ in the interior case and lies in $[0,\pi]$ in the boundary case. This holomorphic coordinate change preserves the equation and Dirichlet energy: $$v_\sigma+J(-e^{-\sigma-i\tau},v)v_\tau=0,\qquad \int_{\sigma>S}(|v_\sigma|_g^2+|v_\tau|_g^2)<\infty,$$ with that tail integral tending to zero as $S\to\infty$. The composed coefficients have uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order; positive cylindrical source derivatives of $-e^{-\sigma-i\tau}$ are bounded and tend to zero. Their restriction to $L$ on the two physical boundary edges is the fixed structure $J(0,x)$, so [F1] applies uniformly on fixed-radius cylinder disks or boundary half-disks. Choose their radius smaller than $\pi/8$. Every point is covered by an interior estimate or a boundary half-radius estimate on such a patch. For sufficiently large $S$ the patch energies are below the fixed threshold, and [F1] gives $$\sup_{\tau}|dv(\sigma,\tau)|_g\longrightarrow0\quad(\sigma\to\infty).$$ This argument uses target-global estimates and assumes no prior containment in one target chart. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We first construct convenient finite-dimensional target data. Take finitely many coordinate charts $U_i$ and smaller relatively compact chart neighborhoods covering $X$. Euclidean smooth bumps supported in $U_i$, equal to one on those smaller neighborhoods, normalized by their positive sum, give a finite smooth partition $\phi_i$. The map $$F:X\longrightarrow\mathbb R^N,\qquad F(x)=(\phi_i(x),\phi_i(x)x_i(x))_i$$ is smooth, interpreting each coordinate product as zero off its compact support. It is injective: if $F(x)=F(y)$ choose $i$ with $\phi_i(x)>0$; the equal first coordinates and coordinate products give $x_i(x)=x_i(y)$. Its derivative is injective by the same argument: if $dF(v)=0$, then $d\phi_i(v)=0$ for all $i$, and at such an $i$ the product derivative gives $\phi_i dx_i(v)=0$. Compactness makes $F$ a homeomorphism onto its image, and [F3] in local coordinates gives smooth inverse charts on that image. Thus $F$ is a smooth embedding. Its induced derivative norms are uniformly equivalent to the original metric norms. No general embedding theorem is needed. [F3, given, construct, algebra]

6.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The coordinate chain rule needed in step 5.1 follows by smooth mollification on smaller patches: continuity gives uniform convergence of coefficient compositions and the weak derivatives converge in $L^2$, so the classical smooth chain rule passes to distributions. Thus the transformed coefficients remain smooth, the boundary plane remains totally real, and all hypotheses of [F2] hold. That lemma proves a smooth extension, including the boundary case. Its boundary value lies in $L$ by step 4.1. The extension adds no energy, since its new point has measure zero. [F2, step 5.1, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Put $w=V_\tau$. It has zero angular mean because $V$ is periodic, and $\Delta w=\partial_\tau H$ because derivatives of a smooth Euclidean map commute. Twice differentiating $e=\tfrac12\int|w|^2$ and integrating by parts only in the periodic angular direction gives $$e''=\int_0^T\bigl(|w_\sigma|^2+|w_\tau|^2-\langle w_\tau,H\rangle\bigr)d\tau.$$ There are no endpoint terms in this integration. By step 2.1 and Young's inequality this is at least $$\int_0^T|w_\sigma|^2+\tfrac12|w_\tau|^2-\tfrac12 C_3^2\varepsilon^2|w|^2\,d\tau.$$ Let $\lambda=(2\pi/T)^2$ and choose $\varepsilon>0$ so that $C_3^2\varepsilon^2\le\lambda/2$. Then [F2] gives $e''\ge(\lambda/4)\int|w|^2=(\lambda/2)e$. Set $c=\sqrt{\lambda/2}$. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Let $h(\sigma)=e(a)e^{-c(\sigma-a)}+e(b)e^{-c(b-\sigma)}$. It satisfies $h''-c^2h=0$ and dominates $e$ at both endpoints. If $e-h$ had a positive value, it would have a positive interior maximum; there its second derivative is nonpositive, contrary to $(e-h)''\ge c^2(e-h)>0$. Thus $e\le h$ throughout the cylinder, giving the claimed pointwise exponential bound. The argument also covers vanishing endpoint values, since $e$ is nonnegative and smooth. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph:
Let $H=\Delta V$, taking the ordinary flat source Laplacian componentwise. The composition rule and [F1] give $$H=dF(
abla_\sigma u_\sigma+
abla_	au u_	au)+(
abla dF)(u_\sigma,u_\sigma)+(
abla dF)(u_	au,u_	au).$$ Uniform coefficient and embedding bounds therefore give $|H|\le C_0(|du|_g+\kappa)|du|_g$. The original equation and the bound for $J$ give $|du|_g\le C_1|u_	au|_g\le C_2|V_	au|$. After imposing the stated smallness, $$|H|\le C_3\varepsilon|V_	au|.$$ This is a pointwise estimate on actual maps into $X$; no ambient extension of $J$ or model moduli equation is assumed. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Choose a finite chart cover and smooth subordinate functions $\phi_i$ with compact supports in those charts and sum one, obtained by Euclidean bumps and normalization. The map $F(x)=(\phi_i(x),\phi_i(x)x_i(x))_i$ is a smooth embedding: at an index where $\phi_i>0$, equality of the displayed coordinates recovers the original chart point, and vanishing of all their derivatives recovers a zero tangent vector. Compactness makes it a homeomorphism onto its image and makes its differential uniformly comparable with the metric $g$. Its first and second covariant derivatives have uniform bounds. This fixes $F$ independently of the cylinder and its map. [given, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The equation and uniform metric comparability give $$E_g(u;[a+R,b-R]\times S_T^1)\le C_4\int_{a+R}^{b-R}e(\sigma)d\sigma.$$ Integrating the two exponentials from step 4.1 bounds the last integral by $c^{-1}(e(a)+e(b))e^{-cR}$. Finally $|V_\tau|\le C|u_\tau|_g\le C\varepsilon$, so $e(a)+e(b)\le CT\varepsilon^2$. This proves all assertions, including uniform decay of central neck energy. A boundary neck has angular endpoint terms and is not covered by the periodic argument. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

Set $w=V_\tau$ and $e(\sigma)=\tfrac12\int_{-T}^T|w|^2d\tau$. The function $w$ is continuous and piecewise smooth, its angular derivative is an ordinary bounded piecewise function locally, and it has zero angular mean. Moreover $\Delta w=\partial_\tau H$ as distributions. Tangential differentiation of the piecewise formulas gives $$e''=\int_{-T}^T\bigl(|w_\sigma|^2+|w_\tau|^2-\langle w_\tau,H\rangle\bigr)d\tau.$$ For completeness the last integration by parts is distributional: $w$ is periodic $H^1$ in its angular variable and $H\in L^2$, so convolution on that circle proves $\langle\partial_\tau H,w\rangle=-\int\langle H,w_\tau\rangle$ by passage to the $L^2$ limit. Thus any jumps of $H$ are included, and no angular endpoint term was omitted. The matching tangential derivatives from step 3.1 justify differentiating the integral twice in $\sigma$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Young's inequality and [F2] give, for $\lambda=(\pi/T)^2$, $$e''\ge\tfrac12\int|w_\tau|^2-\tfrac12C_0^2\varepsilon^2\int|w|^2\ge\tfrac12(\lambda-C_0^2\varepsilon^2)\int|w|^2.$$ Decrease $\varepsilon$ so that $C_0^2\varepsilon^2\le\lambda/2$ and set $c=\sqrt{\lambda/2}$. Then $e''\ge c^2e$. The barrier $h=e(a)e^{-c(\sigma-a)}+e(b)e^{-c(b-\sigma)}$ has $h''=c^2h$ and dominates the endpoint values of $e$. A positive interior maximum of $e-h$ would contradict $(e-h)''\ge c^2(e-h)$, so $e\le h$. Its integral on $[a+R,b-R]$ is at most $c^{-1}(e(a)+e(b))e^{-cR}$. [F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We construct a smooth involution $\rho$ on a neighborhood of $L$ in $X$, fixing $L$, whose differential is $+I$ on $TL$ and $-I$ on $J_bTL$. First the ambient normal map $(y,n)\mapsto y+n$ from the Euclidean orthogonal normal bundle of $Y$ has invertible differential along its zero section. By [F3] it has local smooth inverses. It is injective for a uniform small normal radius: otherwise collisions with normal vectors tending to zero have base points converging after a subsequence by compactness; equality of images forces the same base limit, contradicting the local inverse there. The same compactness argument preserves invertible differential on a uniform radius. Projection of these glued inverses to $Y$ gives a smooth ambient retraction $P$ near $Y$ with $dP$ the tangent projection along $Y$. Now on the vector bundle $N_y=dF(J_bT_xL)$ over $y=F(x)\in M$, consider $\Phi(y,v)=P(y+v)\in Y$. At $v=0$ its derivative identifies $T_yM\oplus N_y$ with $T_yY$, since $L$ is totally real. The identical local-inverse and compactness argument gives a diffeomorphism from a uniform small symmetric bundle neighborhood onto a neighborhood of $M$ in $Y$. Conjugating $(y,v)\mapsto(y,-v)$ by this diffeomorphism and then by $F$ defines $\rho$. It is an involution, fixes $L$, and has the claimed differential. On a smaller fixed neighborhood all its first and second derivatives, and its inverse differential, are bounded. [F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Put $V=F\circ\widetilde u$ and let $H=\Delta V$ weakly on the doubled cylinder. There is no line measure in this Laplacian because $V$ and its first derivatives match across the seams; integrating by parts on both sides verifies cancellation. On the original half, the composition formula and [F1] bound $|H|\le C(|du|_g^2+\kappa|du|_g)$. On the reflected half the composition rule for $F\circ\rho$ gives the same bound, with a larger fixed constant from its second derivatives. The equation gives $|du|_g\le C|u_\tau|_g$, and the embedding and reflected inverse differential compare this with $|V_\tau|$ on either side. Hence $$|H|\le C_0\varepsilon|V_\tau|$$ almost everywhere on the entire doubled cylinder. This argument does not assume a globally smooth reflected almost complex coefficient across a seam. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For small enough $\varepsilon$, the entire map lies in that fixed neighborhood: each path $\tau\mapsto u(\sigma,\tau)$ begins on $L$ and has length at most $T\varepsilon$. Define on the doubled angular circle of period $2T$ $$\widetilde u(\sigma,\tau)=\begin{cases}u(\sigma,\tau),&0\le\tau\le T,\\ \rho(u(\sigma,-\tau)),&-T\le\tau\le0,\end{cases}$$ identifying $-T$ and $T$. This is $C^1$ across both seams. Values agree because $\rho$ fixes $L$. Tangential derivatives agree because $u_\sigma\in TL$ there, so $d\rho u_\sigma=u_\sigma$. The equation gives $u_\tau=J_bu_\sigma\in J_bTL$, so the normal reflected derivative $-d\rho u_\tau$ equals $u_\tau$. These identities hold along the whole seam and may also be differentiated in $\sigma$. Thus all tangential derivatives of the values and normal first derivatives match. The doubled map is smooth on each closed side. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: A fixed finite-atlas embedding is obtained as follows. Choose a finite smooth partition $\phi_i$ with compact supports in coordinate charts $x_i$, using finite Euclidean bumps and normalization, and set $F(x)=(\phi_i(x),\phi_i(x)x_i(x))_i$. Equality of these coordinates recovers $x$ in a chart where $\phi_i>0$, and vanishing of their derivatives recovers a zero tangent vector in that chart. Thus $F$ is injective and immersive, and compactness makes it an embedding. Derivatives of $F$ are bounded and its differential uniformly compares $g$ with the ambient Euclidean metric. Write $Y=F(X)$ and $M=F(L)$. [given, construct, algebra]

7.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The original energy is bounded by $C\int e(\sigma)d\sigma$, by the original equation and embedding norm equivalence. The small derivative hypothesis and the fixed reflected derivative bound give $e(a)+e(b)\le C\varepsilon^2$. Substitution in step 6.1 proves the asserted central energy estimate with a uniform constant. This proves boundary neck decay using the actual totally real boundary geometry. It does not address two different submanifolds or construct a bubble-tree decomposition. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Fix the patch radius $r_0$ in the statement, decreasing it if necessary to satisfy the uniform scale restrictions of [F1]. Every point in $[a,b]\times D$ is covered by an interior smaller patch or a boundary half-radius patch of this radius, contained in the extended cylinder. In the angular interval case, points within $r_0/4$ of an edge use the boundary supremum estimate centered at their boundary foot; other points use an interior disk of radius at least $r_0/8$. Their energies are at most $\delta$: if their radii are smaller, each is contained in one stipulated radius-$r_0$ patch. In the angular circle case all points use an interior disk. Choosing $\delta_0$ below the [F1] thresholds gives $$\sup_{[a,b]\times D}|du|_g\le C_0\sqrt\delta.$$ The unit buffer ensures these patches remain in the prescribed source domain even at $\sigma=a,b$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The exponential barrier in [F2] therefore gives $$e(\sigma)\le C_1\delta\bigl(e^{-c(\sigma-a)}+e^{-c(b-\sigma)}\bigr).$$ Its integral on the central interval is at most $C\delta e^{-cR}$, proving the asserted energy bound. The same inequality and $\sqrt{x+y}\le\sqrt x+\sqrt y$ give $$\int_{a+R}^{b-R}\sqrt{e(\sigma)}d\sigma\le C\sqrt\delta e^{-cR/2},\qquad \sup_{[a+R,b-R]}\sqrt e\le C\sqrt\delta e^{-cR/2}.$$ These bounds do not multiply by cylinder length, since the exponential tails are integrated explicitly. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Let $P$ be the fixed angular period of $V$, and $B(\sigma)=P^{-1}\int V(\sigma,\tau)d\tau$. Angular integration and Holder give $$|V(\sigma,\tau)-B(\sigma)|\le C\sqrt{e(\sigma)}.$$ Moreover $|V_\sigma|\le C|V_\tau|$ on each side, by the original equation, bounded $J$, and the fixed reflection differential and its inverse. Thus $$|B'(\sigma)|\le P^{-1}\int|V_\sigma|d\tau\le C\sqrt{e(\sigma)}.$$ For any two central source points, compare their embedded values to their slice averages and integrate this bound for $B'$ between the slices. Step 3.1 proves that the Euclidean diameter of their embedded images is at most $C\sqrt\delta e^{-cR/2}$. This uses no cancellation of angular endpoint terms; the reflected periodic map is used only after its actual construction in [F2]. [F2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Choose $\delta_0$ further so that $C_0\sqrt{\delta_0}$ is below half the small-gradient threshold in [F2], and choose $\kappa_0$ below half its source-variation threshold. All hypotheses of the corresponding neck estimate hold on $[a,b]\times D$. In the boundary case the small derivative bound also places every angular half-loop in the fixed reflection collar, since it starts on $L$ and has length at most $TC_0\sqrt\delta$. Thus the original periodic embedding, or the reflected periodic double in [F2], is genuinely defined. Its angular period is $T$ or $2T$, and its endpoint slice energies obey $e(a)+e(b)\le C_1\delta$, by the derivative estimate in step 1.1 and the fixed differential bounds of $F$ and $\rho$. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Finally the inverse of the fixed compact embedding is uniformly locally Lipschitz in ambient chord distance. Indeed in each smaller image chart its inverse derivative is bounded; compactness gives a uniform closeness scale within one chart. For pairs separated by more than that scale, the diameter of each relevant compact target component enlarges the constant to a global bound. The connected image of our cylinder lies in one target component, and a compact manifold has finitely many components. Consequently $d_g(x,y)\le C|F(x)-F(y)|$ for pairs in that component, with uniform constant. Applying this to step 4.1 gives the asserted target diameter estimate. Hence both energy and image collapse with $R$ as claimed, conditional only on the concrete local-energy and source-variation bounds in the statement. [step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Let $K=L_0\cap L_1$, now nonempty and finite. Choose pairwise disjoint small metric neighborhoods of its finitely many points. By step 2.1 every sufficiently far tail image lies in their union. That tail source $[S,\infty)\times[0,1]$ is connected, its continuous image is connected, and therefore it lies wholly in one of those neighborhoods, say the one about $x_+$. Within that chosen neighborhood the only possible cluster point is $x_+$ by step 2.1 and separation from the other points of $K$. Compactness now implies uniform convergence of the tail image to $x_+$: a sequence failing it would have a different subsequential cluster point. This proves the asserted uniform endpoint convergence; the derivative convergence was established in step 1.1. Uniqueness follows from uniqueness of a limit in a metric space. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Choose a fixed radius $r>0$ less than $1/16$ and the uniform scale restrictions in [F1]. Since the total energy is finite, the tail energy $E(u;[S,\infty)\times[0,1])$ tends to zero. Each point $(s,t)$ with $s>S+1$ is covered by an interior smaller disk or a boundary half-radius patch of fixed radius comparable to $r$, contained in that tail. Points within $r/4$ of a physical edge use the boundary supremum estimate centered at their boundary foot; other points use a fixed smaller interior disk. At the upper edge the orientation-preserving coordinate $(s,t)\mapsto(-s,1-t)$ turns it into a lower half-plane edge and preserves the equation, replacing the source arguments in $J$ only; its boundary structure is still fixed. Thus [F1] applies with uniform constants on every such patch. Once the tail energy is below its threshold, $$\sup_{s>S+1,\,0\le t\le1}|du(s,t)|_g^2\le C E(u;[S,\infty)\times[0,1]).$$ The right side tends to zero. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For the transverse assertion, choose smooth local parametrizations $f_0,f_1$ of $L_0,L_1$ about an intersection point. The derivative of $(a,b)\mapsto f_0(a)-f_1(b)$ in a target coordinate chart is invertible because the two tangent spaces are complementary. By [F2] the zero of this difference is isolated. Thus the compact set $K$ is discrete. An infinite compact set has an accumulation point, which here would again lie in $K$ and contradict isolatedness; equivalently its isolating neighborhoods have a finite subcover. Hence $K$ is finite. At a negative strip end apply the same argument to $v(s,t)=u(-s,t)$, whose equation has almost complex coefficient $-J(-s,t,x)$ and fixed totally real boundary structures $-J_{b,j}$; all norm and energy hypotheses persist. This proves the remaining assertions without presuming a diagonal linear normal form or an exponential rate. [F2, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Expand each coordinate in the real orthonormal basis of [F2]: $$v_j(s,t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_{jn}(s)e^{-i\lambda_{jn}t},\qquad\lambda_{jn}=\pi n-\theta_j.$$ Its real coefficients are smooth in $s$ by differentiating their integral formula. Integration by parts in $t$ has zero real boundary form: at each edge both $v_j$ and the eigenfunction lie in its same real line. Projecting $v_s+iv_t=0$ consequently gives $$a_{jn}'+\lambda_{jn}a_{jn}=0,\qquad a_{jn}(s)=c_{jn}e^{-\lambda_{jn}(s-S)}.$$ Every mode coefficient is square-integrable in $s$ by step 1.1 and the norm-one coefficient functional. Since no $\lambda_{jn}$ is zero, this forces $c_{jn}=0$ whenever $\lambda_{jn}<0$. Parseval at $S$ gives $\sum_{j,n}|c_{jn}|^2=\|v(S,\cdot)\|_2^2<\infty$. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Finally every derivative of $e^{\delta s}v$ up to a fixed order is a finite linear combination of $e^{\delta s}$ times derivatives from step 3.1. Its square is bounded by $C e^{-2(\gamma_+-\delta)s}$ on the tail, integrable because $\delta<\gamma_+$. This proves membership in every claimed weighted $H^k$ space. The argument proves exponential asymptotics of actual strips for the stated exact local geometric choice and supplies no global extension of that choice, index formula, or universal regularity assertion. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: All surviving eigenvalues are positive and at least $\gamma_+$. For any integer $k\ge0$ and $h=s-S\ge1$, $$\sum_{j,n:\lambda_{jn}>0}\lambda_{jn}^{2k}e^{-2\lambda_{jn}h}\le e^{-2\gamma_+h}\sum_{j,n:\lambda_{jn}>0}\lambda_{jn}^{2k}e^{-2(\lambda_{jn}-\gamma_+)}<\infty.$$ The last constant is finite because these eigenvalues are a finite union of arithmetic progressions with spacing $\pi$. Each mixed derivative of order $k$ of a Fourier term has modulus at most $|c_{jn}|\lambda_{jn}^ke^{-\lambda_{jn}h}$. Cauchy-Schwarz and step 2.1 therefore show that the differentiated series converges absolutely and uniformly for $h\ge1$, with supremum at most $C_k e^{-\gamma_+h}\|v(S,\cdot)\|_2$. The same argument at every derivative order permits termwise differentiation on smaller open tails. The undifferentiated series already equals $v$ in $L^2$ on each slice by completeness; continuity identifies it everywhere, including boundary values, and its uniformly convergent derivatives equal the actual derivatives of $v$. Absorbing the fixed factor $e^{\gamma_+S}$ gives the asserted estimates. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Two transverse embedded curves on a compact surface have finitely many intersections. Each crossing is isolated by [F1] applied to the difference of their local parametrizations in a surface chart, whose derivative is invertible by transversality. Their intersection is closed and compact, so the isolating neighborhoods have a finite subcover and the intersection is finite. There are only finitely many pairs of curves. A generator in $T_\alpha\cap T_\beta$ consists of one point on each alpha circle and one on each beta circle, so it is selected from that finite union of crossings; hence $K$ is finite. Its coordinates are distinct because the alpha circles are disjoint. None is a protected point $p$ because those lie off all circles. Thus $K$ avoids the diagonal and the divisors $E_p$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Conversely, if $B$ anticommutes with $J_0$ and has norm less than one, then $I-B$ is invertible and $$J_B=J_0(I+B)(I-B)^{-1}$$ is an almost complex structure. Indeed conjugation of the Cayley factor by $J_0$ replaces $B$ by $-B$ and therefore replaces that factor by its inverse, giving $J_B^2=-I$. The calculation of step 1.2 gives $\omega(v,J_Bv)>0$ for nonzero $v$. Consequently replacing $B$ by $rB$, $0\le r\le1$, joins the prescribed compatible $J_0$ to the original tame $J$ through tame structures, fixing either endpoint exactly. All expressions depend smoothly on the input operators and $r$ because their denominators remain invertible. [step 1.2, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: At a surface crossing $r$, choose parametrizations $a(x),b(y)$ of the two unique local curves with $a(0)=b(0)=r$, in any smooth surface coordinate chart. The map $\Psi(x,y)=a(x)+b(y)-r$ has invertible derivative at zero. Reverse the parameter $y$ if needed to make its orientation positive. By [F1] its inverse is a smooth orientation-positive chart taking the alpha and beta arcs to the real and imaginary axes in $\mathbb C$. Pulling back the standard complex structure from that chart defines a smooth local structure $j_r$. It is compatible with $\eta$: in the chart $\eta=f(x,y)dx\wedge dy$ with $f>0$, so $\eta(v,j_rv)=f|v|^2>0$ and $\eta(j_rv,j_rw)=\eta(v,w)$. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We prove a pointwise interpolation formula. In a real symplectic vector space let $J_0$ be compatible, write $g_0(v,w)=\omega(v,J_0w)$, and let $J$ be any $\omega$-tame complex structure. Set $A=-J_0J$. The operator $A+I$ is invertible: a vector in its kernel would satisfy $Jv=-J_0v$, contrary to positive $\omega(v,Jv)$ for nonzero $v$. Define $B=(A-I)(A+I)^{-1}$. The relation $AJ_0A=J_0$, obtained directly from $J^2=J_0^2=-I$, gives $J_0^{-1}AJ_0=A^{-1}$ and hence $J_0^{-1}BJ_0=-B$. Thus $B$ anticommutes with $J_0$. Also $I-B=2(A+I)^{-1}$ is invertible and $A=(I+B)(I-B)^{-1}$. For $v=(I-B)w$ we have $$\omega(v,Jv)=g_0(v,Av)=g_0((I-B)w,(I+B)w)=|w|_{g_0}^2-|Bw|_{g_0}^2.$$ Tameness therefore gives $|Bw|_{g_0}<|w|_{g_0}$ for every nonzero $w$. The unit sphere is compact, so $\|B\|_{g_0}<1$. No symmetry of $B$ is assumed or needed. [given, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Apply this formula on each $U_x$ with $J_0=J_{0,x}$ and the given background $J_t$. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi_x$ supported compactly in $U_x$ and equal to one on a smaller neighborhood of $x$. Compute $B_t$ from step 1.2 and replace it by $(1-\chi_x)B_t$ in step 2.2. Its norm remains less than one. Where $\chi_x=1$ the resulting structure is exactly $J_{0,x}$, and where $\chi_x=0$ it is exactly $J_t$, so it glues smoothly to $J_t$ outside $U_x$. The finitely many supports are disjoint and avoid every protected set. Thus all modifications can be made simultaneously, are smooth in the family parameter, preserve tameness, and preserve every original value near the diagonal and protected divisors. [step 3.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

Apply the local extraction argument of [F1] to $v_n$ on an exhaustion of $\mathbb C$. Explicitly, diagonally extract limits of energies on a countable basis of disks and of total energies on exhaustion disks. Points at which every such neighborhood has limiting energy at least the epsilon threshold form a finite set: disjoint neighborhoods about any finite selection have total energy bounded by the original global bound, so their number is uniformly bounded. Away from that finite set the actual epsilon estimates give uniform first derivatives on smaller patches; compact target finite nets and a countable dense source set give local uniform convergence, and the actual local bootstrap then gives all derivative bounds and a countable smooth diagonal limit. Remove any exceptional point where a further subsequence has bounded gradients on one neighborhood, repeating at most finitely many times. Thus the remaining finite set $Z$ consists only of genuine gradient blowup points, and $v_n\to v$ smoothly on compact subsets of $\mathbb C\setminus Z$. Further countable extraction gives energy limits on small rational-radius disks about each $z\in Z$. [F1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

7.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: If $v$ is nonconstant, step 1.1 and step 6.1 give $E_g(v)\ge h$ and hence $m_z\le m-h$ for every child. Suppose $v$ is constant. Then $Z$ is nonempty by step 6.1. At any $z\in Z$ there are nearby points with $|dv_n|\to\infty$. The original center $z_n$ maximizes $|du_n|$ on $B_{1/2}$, and all fixed rescaled compact sets eventually lie there. Thus $|dv_n(0)|$ is at least these diverging values, so $0\in Z$. But $E_g(v_n;B_1)=\mu=m-h/2$ implies $m_0\le\mu<m$. If $Z$ had only this one point, step 6.1 would give $m_0=m$, a contradiction. Therefore $|Z|\ge2$; since each child mass is at least $h$, every child is at most $m-h$ in this case as well. This proves the stability and energy-drop assertions. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Put $\mu=m-h/2>0$. For each large $n$ let $\rho_n$ be the smallest radius with $E_g(u_n;B_{\rho_n}(z_n))=\mu$, restricting to a small fixed disk contained in $B_1$. Such a radius exists: radius-zero energy is zero, energy varies continuously with radius, and step 1.2 makes the energy at any sufficiently small fixed radius eventually greater than $\mu$. The first solution is attained by continuity on a compact interval, so no strict monotonicity or uniqueness of all solutions is needed. The same fixed-radius argument gives $\rho_n\to0$. Define $v_n(w)=u_n(z_n+\rho_n w)$. Its domains contain each fixed planar disk eventually and its coefficient converges smoothly there to $J_\infty(0,x)$. Its energy on the unit disk is exactly $\mu$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Each $z\in Z$ has an atom $m_z\ge h$. To see this, repeat the local distance-weighted rescaling construction of step 2.1 in a small disk about that point. Its smooth normalized plane bubble has energy at least $h$ by step 1.1 and at most the atom mass by the disk containment argument of step 1.2. The limit $v$ has finite energy on $\mathbb C\setminus Z$ by exhaustion and the global bound. By [F2] it extends smoothly across the finitely many points of $Z$ and across infinity, hence is an autonomous holomorphic sphere. Annular smooth convergence and this extension show that energy limits on all small disks about each $z$ exist, not just rational ones, by the continuity/sandwich argument of step 1.2. This defines each $m_z$ independently of the chosen small radii. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The diameter estimate in step 4.2 proves the node connection.
