Only countably many local subsequences, finite groups and finite choices were used, so Countable Choice suffices. This establishes bubbled strip breaking compactness with no gluing or low-index exclusion claim. [F1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.3, construct, algebra] ∎

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph:
Cover $X$ by adapted coordinate neighborhoods as follows. At an intersection use a prescribed common linearizing chart. At a point of $L_j$ off the other submanifold use a submanifold chart flattening $L_j$, small enough to avoid the other closed submanifold. Elsewhere use a chart avoiding both. A finite subcover with smaller relatively compact neighborhoods exists by compactness; finite smooth bumps and normalization give a subordinate partition $\phi_i$. On each chart take the coordinate-flat affine connection $
abla^i$. Every such local connection preserves $TL_j$ in tangent directions wherever its chart meets $L_j$, because that submanifold is a linear coordinate subspace there. The affine combination $
abla=\sum_i\phi_i
abla^i$ is a global smooth connection: $\sum\phi_i=1$ gives the connection Leibniz identity. It is torsion-free, since its torsion is the same weighted sum of the zero local torsions, and it satisfies $
abla_vw\in TL_j$ for tangent fields $v,w$ along $L_j$. Terms with compactly supported weights extend smoothly by zero outside their charts. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Make this connection exactly flat on smaller prescribed generator neighborhoods. On each disjoint common linear chart choose a cutoff equal to one on a smaller relatively compact neighborhood and zero off a larger one. Replace $\nabla$ there by the affine combination of its current value and that chart's flat connection, with these weights. Both connections are torsion-free and preserve both tangent subbundles where present, so those properties persist. The finite modifications are disjoint. On a fixed smaller neighborhood of each generator, the resulting connection has zero Christoffel symbols in the prescribed chart. All its coordinate derivatives of any specified finite order are bounded on finite relatively compact covers. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: In a coordinate chart its geodesic equation is $$x'=p,\qquad p'=-\Gamma(x)(p,p).$$ We prove local existence with parameters using only explicit contractions. On a compact coordinate neighborhood and a bounded velocity ball the smooth right side $F(x,p)$ has bounded norm and Lipschitz constant $L$. For a sufficiently small fixed time $h>0$, the integral map $T_\zeta(X)(t)=\zeta+\int_0^tF(X(r))dr$ maps a fixed closed trajectory ball in $C([0,h];\mathbb R^{2d})$ into itself and has contraction constant $hL\le1/2$. Its explicit iterates converge geometrically in the uniform norm to a unique solution. This solution is $C^1$ in time by its integral equation. Uniqueness on overlaps follows by subdividing into intervals where the same contraction estimate applies. No family of arbitrary fixed-point choices is used: the iterates start at the constant trajectory and their limits are unique. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: A uniform small initial velocity gives a geodesic up to time one. On a smaller coordinate neighborhood the estimate $|p'|\le C|p|^2$ gives $$|p(t)|\le\frac{|p(0)|}{1-C|p(0)|t}\le2|p(0)|\qquad(0\le t\le1)$$ when $C|p(0)|\le1/2$. For nonzero $p$ this follows by differentiating $1/|p|$; a solution hitting $p=0$ is the constant solution by local uniqueness, so no missing zero case occurs. The displacement is at most $2|p(0)|$. Choose the velocity radius uniformly small compared with margins of finitely many smaller coordinate neighborhoods. These bounds keep trajectories in their larger charts. Finitely many short intervals of step 3.1 therefore extend every such solution to time one; step 4.1 and composition give smooth dependence and uniform bounds on all fixed-order derivatives. Coordinate solutions agree intrinsically by uniqueness of the transformed geodesic equation. Define $\mathcal E(x,v)$ as the time-one value. Compactness makes one positive radius work for all base points. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For $x\in L_j$, $v\in T_xL_j$, the restricted geodesic equation on $L_j$ is also an ambient solution. In adapted coordinates its normal initial position and velocity vanish, and the normal acceleration stays zero because $\nabla$ preserves $TL_j$ in tangent directions. The short-interval existence construction within that submanifold followed by ambient uniqueness therefore proves $\mathcal E(x,v)\in L_j$. At $v=0$ the solution is constant. Differentiating its equation in the initial velocity gives $\delta p'=0$, $\delta x'=\delta p$, so $d_v\mathcal E(x,0)=I$. On a generator neighborhood with zero Christoffel symbols its solution is exactly $q(x(t))=q(x)+t\,dq_xv$ as long as that segment remains in the flat region. Shrink the base neighborhood and velocity radius uniformly to ensure this for $0\le t\le1$. This proves the claimed exact coordinate addition. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: In local bundle coordinates the derivative of $\Theta(x,v)=(x,\mathcal E(x,v))$ at $(x,0)$ is the block map $(a,b)\mapsto(a,a+b)$, hence invertible. By [F1] it has a local smooth inverse there. Invertibility persists on a uniform smaller neighborhood of the zero section by compactness. Injectivity also holds on some uniform smaller disk bundle: otherwise choose collisions with both vector norms tending to zero; their first coordinates are the same base point, a subsequence of those base points converges, and the local inverse near that zero vector contradicts the collisions. Thus $\Theta$ is an injective local diffeomorphism, hence a diffeomorphism onto its open image, which contains the diagonal. The same argument for its restriction to $TL_j$ gives a local inverse for close pairs in $L_j\times L_j$; uniqueness of the ambient inverse identifies the two, proving the tangent-valued assertion. Finally [F1], step 4.1 and finite relatively compact covers give bounded derivatives at each fixed order for the addition and its inverse on smaller neighborhoods. All constructions used finite covers and explicit countable iterations, so Countable Choice suffices. [F1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra] ∎

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We first describe weak endpoint values needed for extension. If $g,g_t\in L^2$ on a bounded-height strip and $g_t$ is its weak normal derivative, then on almost every vertical line $g$ is a primitive of $g_t$ plus a constant. Indeed Fubini in the weak derivative identity, using a countable dense family of one-dimensional tests, gives that identity on almost every line. Subtract a primitive; the remaining distribution has derivative zero, hence is constant since every integral-zero compact test is the derivative of a compact test. The primitive has a finite endpoint limit because $g_t$ is integrable on a finite interval. Averaging its fundamental-theorem identity in that interval bounds the $L^2$ norm of the endpoint value by $C(\|g\|_2+\|g_t\|_2)$. Thus for $f\in H^k(S)$ every derivative of order at most $k-1$ has such a weak normal endpoint value. Tangential differentiation under reflected formulas is justified by tests cut off close to the edge; those cutoffs acquire no tangential derivative. [given, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The extension operators commute with the weight, since they reflect only $t$. Multiplication by $w^{-1}$ is bounded on $H^k$, $k\le3$, since $w^{-1}\le1$ and its derivatives are bounded; logarithmic derivatives of $w$ through these orders are bounded as well. Thus $H^k_\delta$ embeds continuously in $H^k$. Applying step 3.1 to $wu$ gives the claimed weighted value bound; for first derivatives use $wD_su=D_s(wu)-\delta\rho'wu$ and $wD_tu=D_t(wu)$, proving both the weighted $C^1$ bound and the derivative estimate. For products write $wfg=(wf)g$ and apply step 4.1, using the unweighted norm bound for $g$. More generally any finite product has the analogous estimate with one weighted factor and the others unweighted, which will be used for composition. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For fixed $k\in\{1,2,3\}$ choose the unique real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ satisfying $$\sum_{j=1}^k a_j(-j)^\ell=1\qquad(0\le\ell<k).$$ The Vandermonde matrix is invertible since the nodes $-1,\ldots,-k$ are distinct; these are finite deterministic algebraic choices. For $-\epsilon<t<0$ extend by $\sum_j a_jf(s,-jt)$, and for $1<t<1+\epsilon$ extend by $\sum_j a_jf(s,1-j(t-1))$, choosing $k\epsilon<1/2$. Across each edge all weak normal jets through order $k-1$ match by these identities and step 1.1, also after tangential derivatives of admissible total order. Piecewise integration by parts therefore gives the ordinary reflected weak derivatives through order $k$, with no line atom. Their $L^2$ bounds follow by the finite sum and changes of variable, so the extension is bounded in $H^k$ on the larger strip. Multiply by a fixed smooth vertical cutoff equal to one on $[0,1]$ and supported in $(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)$, and extend by zero to the plane. This gives a bounded linear plane extension $E_k$. No trace or boundary-density theorem was assumed. By [F1] and restriction it also supplies density on the strip of restrictions of smooth plane functions. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

8.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Finally $DQ(u)\xi=[h_z(\cdot,u)-h_z(\cdot,0)]\xi$. Step 6.1 applied to the bracket and the product bound give $\|DQ(u)\|\le C\|u\|_{H^2_\delta}$ on a small bounded ball. Integrate this derivative along the segment from $v$ to $u$ to obtain $$\|Q(u)-Q(v)\|_{H^2_\delta}\le C(\|u\|_{H^2_\delta}+\|v\|_{H^2_\delta})\|u-v\|_{H^2_\delta}.$$ The finite extensions, weak primitive arguments, explicit approximations and norm-convergent operations above use only Countable Choice. This completes the weighted algebra, composition and quadratic-remainder statements, with the genuine $H^3$ rather than $H^1$ topology available for $C^1$ nonlinear map charts. [step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, construct, algebra] ∎

4.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: A zero gives a continuous weak $W^{1,2}$ solution with totally real boundary, so [F4] makes it smooth up to the boundary. Finite energy and its prescribed ends were proved in step 3.1. Conversely every smooth finite-energy strip has the exponential all-order tails of [F4]. Truncate it sufficiently far out by a real cutoff in the exact product generator coordinates to obtain a smooth reference equal to $x_\pm$ on the ends, preserving both linear boundary planes. The inverse local-addition difference between this reference and the original map tends to zero in $H^3_\delta$ as the truncation moves out, because $\delta<\pi/2$ and the tails decay with that spectral rate. It is pointwise tangent on the boundary and thus belongs to the model by step 1.2. For large truncation the strip therefore lies in that actual chart, proving that all smooth finite-energy strips are included. [F1, F4, step 1.2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For a small $H^3_\delta$ ball of $\xi\in\mathcal X_{u_0}$, [F2] makes its supremum small enough for [F1], so $u=\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)$ is a well-defined $C^1$ map with boundary in $L_j$. Both its value and first derivative approach the prescribed ends. For $\delta=0$ the decay follows by localizing the $H^3$ norm on unit longitudinal windows: their norms tend to zero on the tails by integrability, and the fixed local embedding bound in [F2] gives uniform $C^1$ decay. For positive weight the same estimate applies, or directly uses its exponential factor. References have constant ends, so the reference derivative is compactly supported. Thus $du\in L^2$ and the map has finite energy. The pointwise inverse local addition identifies the chart injectively. Conversely its coordinate inverse is $H^3_\delta$ whenever a second chart map is sufficiently close in this topology, by step 1.1 and bounded smooth finite-dimensional inverse coefficients. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The pointwise boundary condition for an $H^3$ section is equivalent to membership in the indicated $H^1$ boundary domain. In fixed product-line coordinates, the forward implication from completion to trace follows from the weak endpoint $L^2$ estimate proved in [F2]; a continuous $H^3$ representative with that trace lies in the closed real plane at every boundary point. Conversely cut a boundary-compatible $H^3$ section off in $s$ in the $H^1$ norm and split it by a real partition in $t$ into two edge pieces and an interior piece. At the lower edge extend the real part evenly and imaginary part oddly; matching real boundary values make this an $H^1$ extension, as verified by the weak primitive and integration-by-parts argument in [F2]. Convolve with a smooth kernel even in the normal variable. The resulting smooth maps have real boundary values and converge in $H^1$. At the upper edge rotate its line to the real line first, reflect about $t=1$, and use the same construction; its piece is supported away from the other edge. The interior piece is convolved away from both edges. Their sum is a compactly supported smooth boundary-compatible approximation in $H^1$. For the variable product planes from [F3] use its smooth scalar gauge first and undo it after approximation. This proves precisely the required $H^1$ membership, without identifying an $H^3$ closure or imposing normal traces. Scalar weights preserve these pointwise planes. [F2, F3, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: This atlas is second-countable. An explicit finite-atlas embedding of $X$ is $F(x)=(\phi_i(x),\phi_i(x)x_i(x))_i$, where $\phi_i$ is a finite smooth partition in coordinate charts; equality or differential vanishing recovers a point or tangent vector in a chart with $\phi_i>0$. Compactness makes it an embedding. Fix a smooth ambient reference $r(s,t)$ equal to $F(x_\pm)$ outside a compact interval. Map our configuration space into the separable Hilbert space $H^3_\delta(S;\mathbb R^N)$ by $u\mapsto F(u)-r$. The local composition estimates show this is continuous in each chart, injective, and has continuous local inverse on its image. For the last assertion, use the smooth inverse local addition and smooth local inverses of $F$ in finite relatively compact target charts; finite cutoffs give bounded coefficient extensions, so step 1.1 applies. Consequently each chart image is open in the subspace topology of this embedding: nearby configurations have an inverse coordinate close in $H^3_\delta$ and satisfy its boundary domain by step 1.2. A subspace of a second-countable metric space is second-countable, so this topology has a countable base. A countable chart subcover can be selected under Countable Choice by choosing one chart containing each basis element that is contained in some chart. This proves the stated configuration manifold properties. No assertion that every arbitrary pointwise constrained rough map has already been approximated in $H^3$ was used or needed. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Construct fixed component right inverses $Q^\pm:H^2\to H^3\cap\mathcal X^1$. The actual component operators are Fredholm by [F3] and surjective by hypothesis. In an $H^1$ orthogonal complement of their kernels the positive lower bound in [F3] gives a unique bounded inverse to each full $L^2$ range, hence a bounded right inverse $L^2\to H^1$. For $H^2$ inputs the higher regularity estimate in [F3] puts its image in $H^3$ with a bounded norm. Restricting produces the claimed $Q^\pm$. Their boundary condition is exactly the $H^1$ domain intersected with $H^3$, not any unproved stronger closure. They are fixed operators, independent of $R$. [F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: In this chart $J_t=i$ and the local addition is coordinate addition. The two tail maps solve $D_0v=0$, so the pregluing error has the exact coordinate expression $$\chi'(s)(v^-(s+R,t)-v^+(s-R,t)).$$ It is supported in the fixed-width join and its derivatives through order two are $O(e^{-\pi R/2})$ by step 1.1. This proves the claimed $H^2$ error bound. The maps $u_R$ have uniform derivatives of every fixed order. They have finite energy, uniform derivative Sobolev bounds at every fixed order, and exponentially decaying ends, because they are two translates of fixed smooth component maps plus this small fixed-width join. Truncating their outer ends gives actual constant-end references and puts them in the configuration space of [F1]. The same local-addition chart construction can be centered at $u_R$: its coefficients have the stated uniform bounds and its end offsets are exponentially Sobolev integrable. Thus [F1] applies with a uniform radius and uniform first and second section derivative bounds. The nonlinear derivative Lipschitz bound follows, with one constant $L$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Choose a fixed $S$ so that both tails adjacent to $y$ lie in a common smaller product chart $q$ for $s\ge S$ on $u^-$ and $s\le-S$ on $u^+$. Write their coordinates $v^-,v^+$, centered at zero. By [F2], every fixed derivative order satisfies $|D^kv^-(s,t)|\le C_ke^{-\pi s/2}$ on the positive tail and $|D^kv^+(s,t)|\le C_ke^{\pi s/2}$ on the negative tail. Let a real smooth cutoff $\chi(s)$ equal one for $s\le-1$ and zero for $s\ge1$. For large $R$ define $u_R$ to equal the two stated translates outside $[-1,1]$, and on that joining region put $$q(u_R)=\chi(s)v^-(s+R,t)+(1-\chi(s))v^+(s-R,t).$$ The smallness of the tails keeps this in the common chart. It is smooth, has the exact two boundary conditions, and is unchanged from its component maps where the cutoff is constant. The entire interval $[-R+S,R-S]$ lies in that same chart after increasing $S$ if necessary. [F2, given, construct, algebra]

3.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We arrange smooth dependence without claiming operator-norm smoothness of translation on a fixed Sobolev space. The actual map $R\mapsto u_R$ is smooth in the configuration topology: its derivatives differentiate the two fixed translates and the fixed cutoff, and every resulting component derivative has finite Sobolev norm by [F2]. Strong continuity and differentiation of these translations follow by smooth approximation and the fundamental theorem in the longitudinal variable. These derivatives have uniform bounds at each fixed order. The local-addition identifications between $u_R^*TX$ and $u_{R_j}^*TX$ for $R$ close to $R_j$ preserve boundary planes and give smooth norm-bounded maps on $H^3$ and $H^2$. In those fixed spaces the explicit local section formulas in [F1] show that $D_R$ depends smoothly in operator norm, with a uniform local Lipschitz bound. Only pointwise smooth coefficient multiplication and bounded first differentiation occur; no conjugation of an arbitrary bounded operator by norm-differentiable translations is being presumed. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

8.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Let $g_R=\mathcal E(u_R,\xi_R)$. It is a zero of the actual section, so [F1] makes it smooth with finite energy and the prescribed end generators. Its actual geometric $H^3\to H^2$ linearization is surjective by step 7.1. The higher Sobolev range agreement in [F3] implies surjectivity of its $H^1\to L^2$ realization as well: its closed $L^2$ range contains the dense $H^2$ target, so is all of $L^2$. Thus it is regular in the original actual operator sense. On each shifted compact core, step 7.1 and the $H^3\subset C^1$ estimate give convergence to the corresponding component in $C^1$. The actual local smooth bootstrap in [F1] gives uniform bounds of every higher order there; any subsequence therefore has a smoothly convergent subsubsequence with that same $C^1$ limit. This proves smooth local convergence of the entire family to $u^-$ and $u^+$ under the two stated opposite translations. Nonconstancy follows because these nonconstant limits are retained. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 7.1, construct, algebra]

6.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Choose a uniform small parameter radius $a>0$ so that the operator difference in those identifications satisfies $\|D_R-D_{R_j}\|M_0\le1/2$ for $|R-R_j|<a$. Use a fixed arithmetic grid of $R_j$ covering a large half-line. At each grid point take the explicitly constructed $Q_{R_j}^{\rm raw}$ from step 5.1. In its fixed bundle coordinates define $$Q_j(R)=Q_{R_j}^{\rm raw}\bigl[I+(D_R-D_{R_j})Q_{R_j}^{\rm raw}\bigr]^{-1}.$$ This is a smooth local right inverse, by the actual Neumann inverse and its differentiability from [F4], with uniform norm after transferring back to the bundle over $u_R$. Choose a smooth nonnegative parameter partition supported in these radius-$a$ intervals by translating one fixed bump and normalizing its locally finite sum. Their weighted sum $Q_R$ is an actual right inverse, since $D_RQ_j(R)=I$ and the weights sum to one. It is smooth in $R$ and has a uniform norm $M$. The construction uses countably many explicit grid points and locally finite sums only. [F4, step 5.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

7.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Now apply the actual Newton theorem [F4] in each local bundle chart to $\mathcal F_R$, its derivative $D_R$, and this specified $Q_R$. Choose a fixed smaller $r$ inside the uniform chart radius with $MLr\le1/2$. The residual $\varepsilon_R\le Ce^{-\pi R/2}$ from step 2.1 eventually satisfies $2M\varepsilon_R<r$. It gives the unique zero correction $\xi_R\in\operatorname{im}Q_R\cap\overline B_r$ and the bounds $$\|\xi_R\|_{H^3}\le2M\varepsilon_R,\qquad \|\xi_R+Q_R\mathcal F_R(0)\|_{H^3}\le2M^3L\varepsilon_R^2.$$ Its smooth-family clause and step 6.1 make the correction smooth in $R$. The corrected derivative remains surjective with a uniform right inverse of norm at most $2M$. These are precisely the claimed exponential estimates and specified-complement uniqueness. [F4, step 2.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Every component kernel section has uniformly controlled exponentially decaying tails. On an exact generator end its coordinates solve $D_0k=0$ with the two product real planes. Expand them in the real basis of [F3]; coefficients satisfy $a'+\lambda a=0$, $\lambda=\pi n-\pi/2$. The $L^2$ condition kills growing modes on the corresponding end. The surviving absolute eigenvalues are at least $\pi/2$. Their coefficients at a fixed end slice have squared sum bounded by $C\|k\|_{H^1}^2$: the slice $L^2$ norm follows from the fundamental theorem for its square on a unit longitudinal neighborhood and Cauchy-Schwarz. Differentiated Fourier sums, bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz and $\sum\lambda^{2q}e^{-2|\lambda|s}$, then give exponential tails in every fixed derivative and Sobolev norm, with constants linear in $\|k\|_{H^1}$. Higher regularity on the compact core is supplied by [F2]. Thus all estimates are uniform over a norm-bounded set of the finite-dimensional kernels. [F2, F3, construct, algebra]

1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We record the elementary kernel stability used for the correction. Let two surjective bounded operators $T,U:X\to Y$ have specified right inverses $Q_T,Q_U$, with their norms and the operator norms uniformly bounded. Put $P_T=I-Q_TT$ and $P_U=I-Q_UU$. On $\ker T$, the map $P_U$ differs from the identity in ambient $X$ norm by at most $\|Q_U\|\|U-T\|$; on $\ker U$, $P_T$ differs similarly. Thus $P_TP_U$ on $\ker T$ and $P_UP_T$ on $\ker U$ differ from their identities by at most $C\|U-T\|$. If this is less than one, both have bounded Neumann inverses. It follows that $P_U:\ker T\to\ker U$ is bijective, with inverse supplied by either composition, and has uniformly bounded inverse. This proof uses actual complementary projections and completeness only, not an appeal to dimension equality. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Define $A_R(k^-,k^+)$ by translating, identifying and multiplying these two sections by the outer cutoffs $\beta_-^R,\beta_+^R$ exactly as in [F1]. It is a uniformly bounded map $K^-\oplus K^+\to H^3$. Exact operator matching gives $$D_RA_Rk=(\partial_s\beta_-^R)k^-_{\rm shifted}+(\partial_s\beta_+^R)k^+_{\rm shifted}.$$ On their transition the component end coordinates are at distance at least $3R/4$ along the respective tails. Step 1.1 and the cutoff derivative bounds therefore give $\|D_RA_Rk\|_{H^2}\le Ce^{-cR}\|k\|$ for some fixed $c>0$. Set $P_R=I-Q_RD_R$ and $\Gamma_R=P_RA_R$. Since $D_RQ_R=I$, this takes values in $\ker D_R$ and differs from $A_R$ by at most $Ce^{-cR}\|k\|$ in $H^3$. All these maps depend smoothly on $R$: on the finite-dimensional kernels translations differentiate fixed smooth exponentially decaying functions, and the remaining operators are the smooth families in [F1]. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: To prove surjectivity, let $\eta\in\ker D_R$ and cut it into component sections $\eta^\pm$ with one cutoff each, exactly as in step 3.1. Exact matching now gives $D^\pm\eta^\pm=(\partial_s\beta_\pm^R)\eta$ in the matching coordinates. Consequently $$\|\eta^\pm-\Pi^\pm\eta^\pm\|_{H^3}=\|Q^\pm D^\pm\eta^\pm\|_{H^3}\le C R^{-1}\|\eta\|_{H^3}.$$ On translating back and multiplying by the outer cutoffs, their squared sum is exactly one, so $$\|\eta-A_RS_R\eta\|_{H^3}\le C R^{-1}\|\eta\|_{H^3}.$$ The operators $P_R$ have a uniform norm, because $Q_R$ and the coefficients of $D_R$ do. Applying $P_R$ and using $P_R\eta=\eta$ yields $\|\eta-\Gamma_RS_R\eta\|\le C R^{-1}\|\eta\|$. The closed Hilbert space $\ker D_R$ is complete; thus $\Gamma_RS_R$ is invertible there by its actual Neumann series for large $R$. Every vector of that kernel is therefore in the image of $\Gamma_R$. Along with step 3.1 this proves the first isomorphism with uniform inverse bound. No index-additivity theorem was assumed. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

3.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Define a uniformly bounded map $S_R:H^3(u_R^*TX)\to K^-\oplus K^+$ as follows. Cut a section by $\beta_-^R$, identify and translate it to the left component and extend by zero as in [F1], then apply $\Pi^-=I-Q^-D^-$; do the corresponding right operation with $\Pi^+$. Each $\Pi^\pm$ is a bounded projection onto its component kernel. When applied to $A_Rk$, the main component is the kernel vector multiplied by the squared corresponding cutoff; the lost far tail is exponentially small by step 1.1. The other component contributes only in the long cutoff overlap, where that component kernel is exponentially small. Thus $$\|S_RA_R-I_{K^-\oplus K^+}\|\le Ce^{-cR}.$$ Since $S_R$, $Q_R$ are uniformly bounded and $D_RA_R$ is exponentially small, also $\|S_R\Gamma_R-I\|\le Ce^{-cR}$. For large $R$ this is less than one, so its Neumann inverse is bounded. Hence $\Gamma_R$ is injective and has a uniform lower norm bound. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

1.3.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The actual component kernel is spanned by $u_s^\pm$. Translation invariance of the equation gives these kernel sections, their nonzero norm follows from nonconstancy, and their exponential tails put them in every indicated Sobolev realization. Surjectivity and index one make each kernel one-dimensional. Choose smooth compactly supported real test covectors $\psi^\pm$ on the component cores with $\ell^\pm(u_s^\pm)=1$, where $\ell^\pm(k)=\int\psi^\pm(k)$. Explicitly use a nonnegative compact cutoff times the metric dual of $u_s^\pm$, divided by its positive squared integral. Translate these tests to the two cores of $g_R$, using the fixed local-addition identifications, and call their pair $\ell_R$. Its operator norm on geometric $H^3$ is uniform. By [F2] it maps the actual two-dimensional kernel at $g_R$ isomorphically to $\mathbb R^2$, with a uniform inverse bound: on the glued copies of $(u_s^-,0),(0,u_s^+)$ its matrix is $I+O(e^{-cR})$. All harmless tangent identifications between the preglued and corrected maps differ by $O(\epsilon_R)$ on these compact tests. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The corrections also have the differentiated estimates $\|\xi_R'\|_{H^3}+\|\xi_R''\|_{H^3}\le C\epsilon_R$ in these local coordinates. Indeed write $e_R=\mathcal F_R(0)$, $N_R(\xi)=\mathcal F_R(\xi)-e_R-D_R\xi$, and $\xi_R=Q_R y_R$. The fixed-point equation of [F4] is $y_R=-e_R-N_R(Q_Ry_R)$. The exact error in [F1] and its first two $R$ derivatives are $O(\epsilon_R)$ in $H^2$. The explicit local section formulas give, uniformly on a fixed small ball, $\|N_R(\xi)\|+\|\partial_R N_R(\xi)\|+\|\partial_R^2N_R(\xi)\|\le C\|\xi\|^2$, $\|d_\xi N_R(\xi)\|+\|\partial_Rd_\xi N_R(\xi)\|\le C\|\xi\|$, and bounded second $\xi$ derivative. To justify the parameter estimates, subtract the value and the linear term at zero before differentiating the coefficient formulas; each remaining Taylor term has at least two variation factors. Their $H^2$ products are bounded by the actual Sobolev algebra in [F3]. Now $\|y_R\|_{H^2}=O(\epsilon_R)$ follows from its equation and [F1]. Differentiating once gives $(I+d_\xi N_R Q_R)y_R'=-e_R'-\partial_RN_R-d_\xi N_R Q_R'y_R$. Its inverse has norm at most two for large $R$, and the right side is $O(\epsilon_R)$. Differentiate again; its highest unknown is the same invertible factor times $y_R''$, all other terms being $e_R''$, quadratic terms in $y_R,y_R'$ and bounded $Q_R',Q_R''$. They are $O(\epsilon_R)$. The product rule for $Q_Ry_R$ proves the claim. All differentiations are legitimate by the actual smooth parameter conclusion of [F4]. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

1.5.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Fix a smooth target metric and use the translation-invariant energy density $e(u)=\tfrac12(|u_s|^2+|u_t|^2)$. Define $A^\pm(b)=\int_{[b-2,b+2]\times[0,1]}e(u^\pm)$. These smooth nonnegative functions decay with all derivatives at both infinities and have positive maxima. By [F5] choose $0<\delta<\min(\max A^-,\max A^+)$ which is a regular value of both functions. Each level set $(A^\pm)^{-1}(\delta)$ is finite: it is compact by the end decay, and its points are isolated by nonzero derivative, so an infinite set would have an accumulation point contradicting that same derivative condition. Choose a fixed $S$ containing all these crossings and sufficiently large that $A^\pm<\delta/4$ outside $[-S,S]$. Let $b_-$ be the first crossing of $A^-$ and $b_+$ the last crossing of $A^+$. These choices only use a common regular value, finite minima and maxima. [F1, F5, construct, algebra]

1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: We record carefully the smoothness of translation on the regular zero manifold. For each integer $k\ge3$, the construction of [F3] extends to $H^k\cap\mathcal X^1\to H^{k-1}$. The normal extension is the same finite reflected linear combination with coefficients satisfying $\sum_j a_j(-j)^\ell=1$ for $0\le\ell<k$, a nonsingular Vandermonde system. It matches precisely the weak derivatives through order $k-1$ and adds no boundary condition. The $H^2$ algebra and $H^k\subset C^{k-2}$ give the higher product bounds: in a derivative of a product of total order $k\ge3$, at most one factor has order greater than $k-2$, so that factor is estimated in $L^2$ and the others in $L^\infty$. The low order $H^2$ case is already [F3]. Taylor's integral formula gives smooth composition and the actual higher chart and section formulas, with the same zeroth boundary trace argument. At any fixed smooth regular zero the higher operator is surjective by [F3], has the same finite-dimensional kernel, and has a bounded right inverse obtained by restricting its $H^1$ inverse and using the higher regularity estimate. Apply [F4] at orders $3$ and $k$. Inclusion of the higher zero chart into the $H^3$ zero chart has derivative the identity on this common kernel. The finite-dimensional inverse theorem, or the contraction proof of [F4] on that finite-dimensional kernel, makes this inclusion a local smooth diffeomorphism. Thus every local smooth family in the $H^3$ regular zero manifold is locally smooth in every $H^k$ topology. Translation of such a family is then smooth into $H^3$: its $a$ derivatives are longitudinal derivatives, and any prescribed finite order is controlled by taking a sufficiently high $k$. The translation difference quotients converge by the fundamental theorem and smooth approximation, as in [F1]. This is a statement on the actual regular zero manifold; it does not assert norm differentiability of translation on all $H^3$ maps. [F3, F4, construct, algebra]

5.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Separation of the first and last energy-window crossings is invariant under translation. Hence $\tau_a g_R=\tau_{a'}g_{R'}$ implies $T(R)=T(R')$, so $R=R'$ by step 3.2. Then $g_R$ would have longitudinal period $a-a'$ if these translations differed. A nonconstant smooth periodic strip has positive energy on one period (zero energy would make both derivatives identically zero), and summing its disjoint period translates contradicts finite total energy. Thus $a=a'$. This proves the global injectivity and uniqueness asserted in the statement. The local diffeomorphism of step 4.1 is in the actual two-dimensional regular zero manifold because [F2] gives kernel dimension two and [F4] gives its actual local zero charts. Translation is free by the same finite-energy argument, and the local phase charts give actual local quotient coordinates. Consequently the injective map $R\mapsto[g_R]$ is a smooth local coordinate there. [F1, F2, F4, step 4.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Put $\epsilon_R=e^{-\pi R/2}$. We first choose the right inverses with uniform bounds on their first two parameter derivatives in the moving bundle coordinates of [F1]. In its construction, the coefficients of $D_R$, the local-addition identifications and their first two $R$ derivatives have uniform bounds: they differentiate translates of fixed smooth component maps, with uniformly bounded derivatives and integrable tails, and a fixed joining cutoff. Fix a parameter radius $a>0$ for the local Neumann formula, uniformly small so its denominator has inverse norm at most two. At arithmetic grid points $R_j$ use the already constructed right inverses of uniform norm. On $|R-R_j|<a$ the formula is $Q_j(R)=Q_j(R_j)[I+(D_R-D_{R_j})Q_j(R_j)]^{-1}$ in the fixed local spaces. Differentiating the Neumann inverse twice gives uniform bounds in terms of the first two coefficient derivatives and the fixed inverse bound. Transfer back using the same bounded smooth bundle identifications. Average these exact right inverses with translates of one fixed parameter bump divided by their locally finite sum. The overlap number and derivatives of this partition are uniformly bounded. Thus $Q_R,Q_R',Q_R''$ are bounded independently of $R$. Replacing the original smooth choice by this specified choice preserves all conclusions of [F1] and [F2]. [F1, F2, F4, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For $H_R(a,\rho)=\tau_a g_{R+\rho}$, evaluate the difference from $g_R$ with these same two phase tests, using the centered coordinate $\mathcal E_{u_R}^{-1}(H_R(a,\rho))-\xi_R$. At $(a,\rho)=(0,0)$ the phase derivative matrix is $$\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}+O(\epsilon_R).$$ On the left core the pregluing is $u^-(s+R,t)$, so both a longitudinal translation and increasing $R$ differentiate to $u_s^-$; on the right core increasing $R$ differentiates to $-u_s^+$ while translation differentiates to $u_s^+$. Step 2.1 bounds the correction's $R$ derivative in $H^3$, and its longitudinal derivative in $H^2$ is $O(\epsilon_R)$; hence the phase errors have the stated bound. The second derivatives of these scalar phase expressions are uniformly bounded for uniformly small $a,\rho$: the terms use two longitudinal derivatives of $g_R$, one longitudinal derivative of $\partial_Rg_R$, or $\partial_R^2g_R$, all bounded in $L^2$ on the fixed tests by [F1] and step 2.1. The local-addition inverse coefficients and derivatives are uniformly bounded there. By step 1.2 the expressions are smooth. Thus the finite-dimensional contraction argument gives a fixed parameter neighborhood on which this phase map is injective and covers a fixed ball. Step 3.1 keeps the corresponding maps within the uniform zero chart from step 2.2, after shrinking this neighborhood once. Comparing their phases in that zero chart shows that every actual zero sufficiently close to $g_R$ equals a unique $\tau_a g_{R+\rho}$ with small $a,\rho$. This proves a uniform local diffeomorphism and uniform local exhaustion. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 3.1, step 1.3, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

5.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Since $g_{T_n}$ differs from $u_{T_n}$ by $O(\epsilon_{T_n})$, the chart transition estimates in [F3] turn step 1.4 into $H^3$ closeness to $g_{T_n}$. Apply the uniform phase exhaustion of step 4.1 to get $v_n=\tau_{\alpha_n}g_{T_n+\rho_n}$ with $\alpha_n,\rho_n\to0$. The convergence of these parameters follows quantitatively from the uniform inverse phase derivative and the phases tending to zero. Undoing $v_n=\tau_{d_n}w_n$ gives $w_n=\tau_{\alpha_n-d_n}g_{T_n+\rho_n}$. Thus the asserted parameter asymptotics and eventual representation are proved. At this point uniqueness holds within each local parameter neighborhood; global uniqueness is proved next. [F1, F3, step 4.1, step 1.4, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Construct a countable collection $B_n$ of smooth endomorphism fields compactly supported in $O$, anti-commuting with $J^*$, whose finite span is dense in every finite $C^k$ norm on smooth compactly supported such fields. Fix a finite smooth coordinate atlas on $X$ and its induced local tangent frames, and rational product-coordinate balls with compact closure inside $O$ and one such atlas chart. In each ball take the fixed smooth bump $\varphi((z-q)/r)$, for rational center $q$ and positive rational radius $r$, times each real matrix unit of the local frame; extend by zero and apply the smooth fiber projection $A\mapsto(A+J^*AJ^*)/2$. These are countably many fields and anti-commute with $J^*$. To verify density, split any given compactly supported field by a finite smooth partition subordinate to such relatively compact charts; an ordinary finite partition follows by finitely many bumps positive on its compact support and dividing their sum. Its local coefficient functions extend smoothly by zero. Convolution with the normalized bump at rational radii tending to zero converges with every prescribed finite number of derivatives, because differentiation commutes with convolution and the derivatives are uniformly continuous on a compact support. Each convolution integral is approximated in $C^k$ by finite Riemann sums with rational centers: uniform continuity of the derivatives of the translated bump gives convergence of the same finite sums for all derivatives through order $k$. Approximate the finitely many coefficients by rational numbers if desired. The supports remain in the chosen chart and $O$ when the radius and the grid are small enough. The resulting finite combinations of the enumerated matrix bumps approximate the local field, and the smooth projection preserves convergence and fixes the original anti-commuting field. Summing the finite partition proves the assertion. At any $p\in O$, a rational ball containing $p$ with positive bump value supplies all projected matrix units there, so their evaluations span the full anti-$J^*(p)$ fiber. Zero or repeated entries may be included to obtain one sequence indexed by $\mathbb N$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: Fix global coefficient $C^k$ norms using the finite atlas on the compact manifold $[0,1]\times X$. Put $$c_n=\frac{2^{-n}}{1+\max_{0\le j\le n}\|B_n\|_{C^j}},\qquad B(a)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_nc_nB_n.$$ For each fixed $k$, $\sum_n c_n^2\|B_n\|_{C^k}^2<\infty$: its tail $n\ge k$ is bounded by $\sum_n4^{-n}$ and its preceding terms are finite. Cauchy–Schwarz therefore gives convergence of every derivative through order $k$, uniformly, with norm at most $C_k\|a\|_{\ell^2}$. The compatible uniform derivative limits are the derivatives of the limiting field, by the coordinate fundamental theorem applied successively. Thus $B(a)$ is smooth, anti-commutes with $J^*$, and defines a bounded linear map $H\to C^k$ for every $k$. Every term vanishes on $P$, hence so does the limit. Derivatives vanish there as well, though equality of values suffices. In particular the sum vanishes on the same fixed endpoint collars; this is stronger than merely summing bumps each with its own possibly shrinking collar. The positive constants $c_n$ leave the finite span and all pointwise spanning conclusions unchanged. Separability and completeness of the real sequence Hilbert space follow from truncation to finitely many coordinates with rational entries and the coordinatewise limit of any Cauchy sequence, whose squared tail bounds pass to the limit. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: The tangent-density assertion holds at every parameter, not only at zero. Write $B=B(a)$ and $R=(I-B)^{-1}$. Differentiation gives $$dJ[C]=2J^*RCR.$$ This is a linear isomorphism from the anti-$J^*$ fiber to the anti-$J(a)$ fiber. One can verify invertibility either directly with inverse $C=-\tfrac12(I-B)J^*Y(I-B)$ or by differentiating the inverse coordinate formula $B=(A-I)(A+I)^{-1}$, where $A=-J^*J$. These formulas are defined in the same norm neighborhood and preserve the anti-commuting identities by multiplication. They also give bounded smooth coefficient isomorphisms in each finite $C^k$ norm and preserve compact support. Thus step 1.1 applied to the inverse image of a compactly supported $Y$ proves tangent density, and its pointwise spanning assertion proves fiber surjectivity. Finally for a nonzero $v$, any prescribed $w$ is $Yv$ for some anti-$J(a)$ endomorphism: on the real plane spanned by $v,J(a)v$ prescribe $Yv=w$, $YJ(a)v=-J(a)w$, and set $Y=0$ on its $J(a)$-invariant orthogonal complement for the invariant metric $g+g(J(a)\cdot,J(a)\cdot)$. The plane is two-dimensional because $J(a)^2=-I$. Consequently parameter evaluation on $v$ is onto, with a finite-support parameter vector for each such prescribed value. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

7.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: All analytic constructions are actual smooth fields, convergent Hilbert series, explicit local section formulas and specified finite-dimensional lifts. What remains for universal transversality is the substantive assertion that the universal derivative is onto at the desired zeros. The pointwise spanning result of step 4.1 only applies at $(t,u(s,t))\in O$; it cannot supply a variation at a protected point or at an entire fixed endpoint collar. In particular countably many unrestricted interior bump supports cannot replace this construction while retaining an actual common endpoint collar. Proving that each relevant strip has an available injective point, or proving regularity by a separate argument when none is available, remains necessary. These limitations do not alter any of the actual family, density or universal local-setup conclusions just proved. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct] ∎

6.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: At a zero write $E=H^3\cap\mathcal X^1$, $Y=H^2$, $P_0=P_{a,u}$ and $K:H\to Y$ for the bounded parameter derivative. The actual $P_0$ is Fredholm by [F1] and [F2]. Let $C=Y/\operatorname{Ran}P_0$, a finite-dimensional quotient, and $q:Y\to C$ its quotient map. The universal derivative has range $q^{-1}(\operatorname{im}(qK))$, closed because every subspace of the finite-dimensional $C$ is closed. If it is onto, choose finitely many parameter vectors whose $qK$ images form a basis of $C$; this is finite choice. They give a bounded linear right inverse $j:C\to H$ to $qK$. The fixed operator $P_0$ has a bounded inverse on an $H^1$ kernel complement to its closed range by [F2], and its restriction maps $H^2\cap\operatorname{Ran}P_0$ boundedly to $H^3$ by the higher estimate there. Denote this range inverse by $Q_0$. Then $$f\longmapsto\bigl(jqf,\ Q_0(f-Kjqf)\bigr)$$ is a specified bounded right inverse of the actual universal derivative. Apply [F3] to get its actual local separable Hilbert zero chart. Its tangent space is $\{(b,\xi):P_0\xi+Kb=0\}$. Projection to $H$ has kernel $\ker P_0$ and image $\ker(qK)$, so its cokernel is isomorphic to $C$ because $qK$ is onto. It is Fredholm with index $\dim\ker P_0-\dim C=\operatorname{ind}P_0$. That projection derivative is onto exactly when $C=0$, which is equivalent to $P_0$ onto. Countable local charts follow from the second-countable product in [F1] and the separable parameter space, using Countable Choice if a chart subcover is selected. No claim that the displayed right inverse exists when the universal derivative is not onto has been made. [F1, F2, F3, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

1.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: First prove the elementary constant-principal weak estimate on the plane. If $w\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C^m)$ has compact support and $D_0w=f\in L^2$ distributionally, convolve with one fixed smooth compactly supported approximate identity to obtain smooth compactly supported $w_\varepsilon$ with $D_0w_\varepsilon=f_\varepsilon$. Such convolution converges in $L^2$: translation is continuous first for rectangular step functions by their symmetric-difference measure, then for all $L^2$ functions by their step-function approximation; the integral of the translation differences is bounded by their supremum over the shrinking convolution support. The same argument treats $f$. For smooth compactly supported maps integration by parts gives $$\|D_0w_\varepsilon\|_2^2=\|(w_\varepsilon)_s\|_2^2+\|(w_\varepsilon)_t\|_2^2.$$ Indeed $\int\langle w_s,iw_t\rangle_{\mathbb R}$ is zero: integration first in $s$ and then in $t$, and skew symmetry of $i$, show it equals its negative. Thus the derivative norms are bounded by $\|f\|_2$, since convolution with a normalized nonnegative kernel is $L^2$ contractive by Cauchy–Schwarz and integration. For each compactly supported smooth real test $\phi$, pass to the limit in $\int w_\varepsilon\partial_j\phi$ to get a bounded functional of $\phi$ in its $L^2$ norm, of bound $\|f\|_2$. The bounded-test Hilbert representation argument in [F2] supplies the weak derivative in $L^2$ without selecting a weakly convergent subsequence. Apply the same bounded-test argument simultaneously to a pair of tests for the two derivatives: Cauchy–Schwarz bounds their combined functional by $\|f\|_2$ times the product $L^2$ test norm. Hilbert representation in that product space therefore gives $w\in H^1$ and $\|\nabla w\|_2\le\|f\|_2$. Repeating this argument for each distributional $\partial^\alpha w$ shows that if $w\in H^q$ and $D_0w\in H^q$, then $w\in H^{q+1}$ with $\|w\|_{H^{q+1}}\le C_q(\|D_0w\|_{H^q}+\|w\|_2)$. Each derivative is compactly supported, so the same argument applies. [F2, construct, algebra]

4.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: A closed subspace of the real Hilbert $L^2$ space equals all of $L^2$ precisely when its orthogonal complement is zero, by the Countable-Choice orthogonal projection in [F2]. The orthogonal complement of $\operatorname{Ran}A_0$ is exactly the sections annihilating both $P E_0$ and $K_0H$, since those two subspaces add to that range. Step 3.1 makes every such obstruction smooth in the interior. Combined with step 1.3 this proves the claimed exact obstruction criterion at both Sobolev levels. All weak limits were obtained from bounded tests and Hilbert representation, with only finite coordinate reductions and explicitly prescribed convolutions; no stronger choice axiom or unproved adjoint regularity theorem was imported. Unique continuation, the existence of a free injective point and the final elimination of these actual smooth interior obstructions remain separate statements. [F2, step 3.1, step 1.3, construct, algebra] ∎

1.2.exact_current_proof_paragraph: A smooth variable complex principal part reduces exactly to this constant one locally. Let $K(z)^2=-I$ and $v_s+K(z)v_t+C(z)v=0$ distributionally, with $v\in L^2_{\rm loc}$ and $K,C$ smooth. At a point choose a constant real basis identifying $K(z_0)$ with standard multiplication $i$. Such a basis is obtained by successively taking a nonzero vector and its $K(z_0)$ image, then passing to the invariant orthogonal complement for the metric $g+g(K(z_0)\cdot,K(z_0)\cdot)$; only finitely many choices occur. In these coordinates put $\Phi(z)=(I-K(z)i)/2$. Then $K\Phi=\Phi i$ and $\Phi(z_0)=I$, so it is invertible on a smaller neighborhood. Writing $v=\Phi h$ gives $$D_0h+B h=0,\qquad B=\Phi^{-1}(\Phi_s+K\Phi_t+C\Phi),$$ with smooth $B$. Multiplication and the product rule for smooth coefficients and distributions justify the same formula for $L^2$ solutions, not only smooth ones. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For nested relatively compact neighborhoods choose a cutoff $\chi$ supported in the larger one and equal to one in the smaller one. The section $w=\chi h$, extended by zero to the plane, satisfies $D_0w=-\chi Bh+(D_0\chi)h\in L^2$. Step 1.1 puts it in $H^1$ and bounds its norm by a constant times the $L^2$ norm of $h$ on the larger neighborhood. If $h\in H^q$ locally, the same cutoff equation has right side in $H^q$, with norm bounded by finitely many derivatives of $B,\chi$ times $\|h\|_{H^q}$ on a slightly larger compact set. Apply the last assertion of step 1.1 to get the next derivative, using a fresh nested cutoff. Induction gives every local $H^q$ estimate by the original $L^2$ norm. Multiplication by $\Phi,\Phi^{-1}$ preserves these estimates with constants depending on their finite derivative bounds. Finally for any derivative order $j$, a compactly supported localization of $\partial^j h$ belongs to $H^2$, so the actual local $H^2\subset C^0$ estimate in [F1] gives a continuous representative. These representatives are compatible weak derivatives; their first derivative identities imply ordinary differentiability by mollification and the coordinate fundamental theorem. Induction gives a smooth representative. A finite covering of compact subsets combines the estimates. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

1.3.exact_current_proof_paragraph: For the range assertions, put $Y_0=L^2$, $Y_2=H^2$, $E_0=H^1\cap\mathcal X^1$, and $E_2=H^3\cap\mathcal X^1$. Let $q_i:Y_i\to Y_i/\operatorname{Ran}P_i$ be the quotient maps for the actual realizations $P_i:E_i\to Y_i$. These ranges are closed of finite codimension by [F2]. Each augmented range is $$\operatorname{Ran}A_i=q_i^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{im}(q_iK_0)\bigr),$$ because an output has this quotient exactly when its difference from some $K_0b$ is in the fixed-parameter range. The image on the right is a subspace of a finite-dimensional quotient, hence closed. Thus both augmented ranges are closed. If $A_0$ is onto, for $f\in H^2$ choose any $(\xi,b)\in E_0\oplus H$ with $P\xi=f-K_0b$. The right side belongs to $H^2$, so actual higher regularity in [F2] puts $\xi$ in $E_2$, proving $A_2$ onto. Conversely if $A_2$ is onto, the closed $L^2$ range of $A_0$ contains all of $H^2$, which is dense in $L^2$ by smooth compact interior approximation. Hence it is all of $L^2$. No identification of an $H^2$-dual annihilator with a function was used. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]
